Short answer and decision: deal with (b) first. Coercing weaker brethren to miss public worship is the more grievous offense because it actively wounds others’ consciences and the congregational worship life; the sabbath-sinners in (a) are culpable and must be corrected, but their sin is private (against God and their own soul) rather than an active scandal and abuse of office that robs others of worship.

Reasoning from the Westminster Standards (esp. WCF ch. 21 on the Lord’s Day; the Larger and Shorter Catechisms on the fourth commandment and Sabbath duties and sins): the Lord’s Day is to be kept holy by public and private worship and resting from ordinary worldly employments. Willful, habitual neglect of that duty is sinful. The Standards also require Christians to love and protect one another in holy living; causing others to be prevented from worship — especially by pressure from someone in authority — is a scandal that injures their consciences and spiritual good, and therefore is a more aggravated breach of duty.

Breakdown of each case

(a) Man who every Lord’s Day habits away the whole day for errands/recreation, skipping worship
- What aggravates it
  - Willful and settled habit: repeated, deliberate neglect rather than occasional failure.
  - Frequency and permanence: “every Sunday” shows hardness of heart and neglect of covenantal duty.
  - Personal example: as a section leader he is a public Christian in the ensemble, so his conduct is also a poor example to others.
- Single most defining feature
  - Persistent personal profanation of the Lord’s Day — a settled refusal to keep the Sabbath holy for worship and rest.

(b) Section leader who requires four young singers to attend a Sunday-morning sectional during the hour of public worship, including two new believers who want to worship
- What aggravates it
  - Abuse of authority: using her control over solos/ensemble membership to compel obedience.
  - Causing others to miss public worship: directly preventing worship by those under her influence.
  - Targeting (effectively) weaker/new believers: it is especially damaging to novices in the faith.
  - Conscience violation and scandal: these members are kept from the very duty Westminster insists on, against their conscience.
- Single most defining feature
  - Active coercion that deprives others of their duty to worship and wounds their consciences — a scandalous offense against neighbor and the corporate worship life.

Decisive moral considerations and ranking (least → most)
- Decide between private sin and public, coercive harm to others: Westminster teaching on the sabbath makes both sinful, but the church has a special duty to prevent scandal and to protect the weak in conscience and their access to worship. A sin that injures others’ souls and the congregation’s worship by use of authority is therefore more heinous than a private habitual profanation (which must nonetheless be corrected).

Practical counsel (what to do this week)
1. Handle (b) immediately (this week)

Aim for repentance and restoration where possible, but be prepared to enforce discipline to preserve order and prevent further scandal.

Ranking, with decisive consideration at each step
- Least heinous — (b): decisive consideration — single outburst mitigated by apology; restoration appropriate.
- Most heinous — (a): decisive consideration — sustained, unrepentant breach of filial duty that covertly undermines authority and trust.

Short answer and decision for today: treat (a) first — it is the graver offence. Reason: (a) is a deliberate, private coercion of conscience that directly hinders the duty and right of the weakest to attend public worship; that kind of abuse of authority and direct denial of worship is the most serious Sabbath-profaning sin here. (b) is also grave (public, scandalous, habitual), and must be dealt with promptly next — it is the more public undermining of the Lord’s Day and of the magistrate’s duty to preserve public worship.

Brief Westminster-based reasoning (with decisive consideration named for each):

(a) The compulsory Sunday-morning shift imposed on vulnerable, new-believing employees
- Aggravating features:
  - It uses the power of office to coerce the conscience of the weak (targeted pressure on low-paid, new believers).
  - It directly prevents attendance at public worship (the very duty the Sabbath requires).
  - It is hypocritical (the supervisor keeps the day for herself while denying it to others).
  - It is regular and intentional rather than occasional necessity or mercy.
- Single most defining feature (decisive consideration): deliberate coercion that causes others to miss public worship and violates their conscience.
- Westminster warrant: WCF 21 requires the Lord’s Day to be set apart for public worship; the Larger Catechism/WSC identifies “causing others” to do ordinary work and “not attending public worship” as Sabbath-profaning sins. The magistrate has special duty to protect public worship and the weak (WCF 23.3).

(b) The supervisor who openly runs the crew on non‑urgent Sunday mornings in the town’s main streets
- Aggravating features:
  - It is public and habitual, seen by the whole church‑attending town (a scandalous example).
  - It is willful and unnecessary (could be done other days), so not a work of necessity or mercy.
  - It involves an official crew and thus a civic endorsement of profanation.
- Single most defining feature (decisive consideration): public, habitual scandal that undermines communal reverence for the Lord’s Day and violates the magistrate’s duty by example.
- Westminster warrant: WCF 21 stresses sanctifying the Lord’s Day by public and private worship; magistrates must restrain public profanation and protect the peace and order of worship (WCF 23).

Practical course of action today (you can only address one properly this week)
- Address (a) this week (first priority). Immediate actions consistent with the WCF’s picture of the magistrate’s duty:
  1. Private but firm intervention today: summon the department head for a clear, documented admonition. Explain that using scheduling authority to bar employees from public worship is forbidden and must stop at once.
  2. Stop the coercion immediately: order the schedules changed so these employees can attend worship; expressly forbid mandatory Sunday shifts except for true emergencies or works of necessity/mercy.
  3. Protect the victims: meet with the affected employees (or a trusted representative) to confirm they may attend worship without retaliation, and offer remediation if they lost wages or were disciplined.
  4. Impose suitable discipline or corrective measures on the supervisor (reprimand, loss of scheduling authority, suspension, or removal if she persists), with record, and require a written apology and assurance of changed practice.
  5. Adopt a clear council policy (or emergency directive): municipal employees may not be compelled into regular Sunday shifts except for emergencies/public necessity; publish it so rights are clear.
  6. If the supervisor resists or this is systemic, proceed under the council’s employment procedures to remove the abusive authority and protect worship rights.

- Plan to address (b) next (early next week)
  1. Issue an immediate stop-order for non‑urgent Sunday work; allow only genuine emergencies/necessities (consistent with WCF 21’s allowance for works of necessity and mercy).
  2. Convene the crew’s supervisor and require cessation, public correction/apology, and a plan to schedule non‑urgent maintenance on other days.
  3. If public example was deliberate or repeated after warning, apply progressive discipline; consider reassigning or removing supervisors who persist in open profanation.
  4. Publish guidance to the town so the community knows municipal practice supports sanctifying the Lord’s Day.

Short pastoral note (brief, in the spirit of the Standards): the magistrate’s calling is both to protect public worship and to guard consciences. Both sins must be corrected; the private, coercive denial of the right to worship is the sharper injury to persons’ souls and consciences and so takes the immediate precedent, while the public, scandalous profanation must follow quickly because it corrupts the common life.

Short answer first: Yes — both the promise you made and the marriage covenant remain morally binding. Your attraction to another woman does not release you from the vow you took before God and your wife. What you must do now is repent, remove temptation, get help, and renew your faithfulness in practical ways.

Reasoning from the Westminster Standards (and the biblical truth on which they rest)
- The Westminster Confession affirms that marriage is a covenant instituted by God and to be held in honor (WCF, ch. 24). It is a lifelong covenantal bond, broken only on scriptural grounds (adultery or desertion as treated in Scripture). Your engagement promise — made seriously and privately before marriage — is a moral commitment that issues from that same covenantal understanding: vows and promises made before God and another are binding.
- The Standards teach the duty of Christians to keep their vows and to live in holy obedience, mortifying sin and practicing the duties of their station (see WCF chs. on vows, sanctification, and the duties of marriage). That includes patience, fidelity, helping one another’s weaknesses, bearing infirmities, and resisting temptation.
- Attraction and temptation are real and common; they are not in themselves the same as adultery, but Scripture and the Standards require that we mortify and flee from lust and guard the marriage (cf. Matthew 5:27–28; WCF emphases on mortification and holiness).

Practical counsel (what to actually do)
1. Own it before God and repent
   - Confess this temptation and any willful indulgence of it to God. Repentance is the Christian’s first step: turning from the sin and turning back to duty and love toward your wife.

2. Cut off the occasion of sin immediately
   - End or reconfigure the friendship with the gym woman so there is no private, emotionally intimate access: no one-on-one workouts, no private messaging, no sharing your marital burdens with her. Create clear, enforceable boundaries now.
   - If that means changing gym times, removing the “gym buddy” routine, or avoiding private contact, do it. The Standards teach fleeing occasions of sin and exercising self-denial.

3. Get accountability and pastoral help
   - Tell a trustworthy pastor, elder, or Christian counselor what’s going on. Do this before confiding widely. A pastor can help you discern whether and how to confess to your wife and can give you accountability to stay away from the other woman.
   - Set up an accountability relationship for phone/text checks, accountability software if needed, and regular meetings with the counselor/elder.

4. Seek marriage and individual help
   - Enter counseling with your wife (and encourage her to get appropriate treatment for the eating disorder, if she’s not already in it). The promise you made involved being her safe person and helper; that is a duty that must be carried by both grace and wisdom — professional treatment for her and pastoral/marital support for both of you.
   - You also may need individual counseling for how to carry the burden without looking for relief outside the marriage.

5. Recommit and repair trust wisely
   - Work with your pastor/counselor about how to speak to your wife. Bluntly confessing “I’m attracted to someone else” without a plan or pastoral care can be wounding and destabilizing. But secrecy and hiding will only deepen sin. Guided confession (with a plan for repentance and boundaries) is usually the wise course.
   - Reaffirm the vow you made — privately first, and publicly or with pastoral affirmation if appropriate — and show by concrete acts that you are keeping it.

6. Practice the duties and the disciplines
   - Renew spiritual disciplines (prayer, Scripture, the sacraments, church fellowship). The Westminster Standards emphasize growth in holiness and the mortification of sin; these are not abstract: regular dependence on God and the means of grace protect and strengthen you.
   - Bear your wife’s burden with patience, but not in isolation. Bring the burden before the church where appropriate and helpful: marriage is not meant to be carried alone.

7. Distinguish responsibility from blame
   - You are not morally excused by the difficulty of your wife’s illness. Christian duty often calls us to bear another’s infirmities (Gal. 6:2; WCF teachings on mutual duties). That does not mean you must be unhealthy or bear abuse or be the only helper; it does mean you must not abandon your vows because the load is heavy. Use the church’s resources to avoid burnout.

A word about timing and wisdom
- Don’t make a crisis out of every passing temptation, but don’t minimize it either. If the attraction has led you to emotional intimacy with the other woman, that is serious and must be confessed and cut off. If it is a temptation you have noticed and repented of, take the concrete boundary steps now and get accountability so you don’t fall.
- Work with a pastor about how and when to tell your wife. Full honesty is necessary in marriage, but the manner and timing should be governed by charity and the goal of healing and reconciliation.

Conclusion
Your promise and marriage remain binding. The gospel calls you to repent of entertaining or cultivating that attraction, to cut off its occasions, to seek pastoral and professional help, to renew your commitment, and to carry the burden with Christian patience but with wise supports in place. The gym buddy’s counsel to treat the vow as void because the situation is hard is not a ground offered by Scripture or the Westminster Standards for release from your promise.

Short answer from the Standards: you keep the wedding booking and you tell the bride honestly about the second song.

Why, theologically and morally (briefly)
- The Westminster Standards teach that the moral law of God continues to bind Christians: keep your word, do justice, and do not defraud your neighbor. The exposition of the eighth commandment in the Larger Catechism requires “the lawful procuring and furthering the wealth and outward estate of ourselves and others” and forbids “unjustly to take, detain, or convert to our own use” what belongs to another. A written booking with a deposit is an obligation you voluntarily undertook.  
- The Standards also treat vows and promises as binding (WCF, ch. 22). Breaking a promise for mere gain is not a lawful or honorable way to act.  
- The ninth commandment forbids lying and deception; thus giving a false reason for cancelling would itself be sinful.

Application to your situation
- The couple booked you in writing and paid a deposit; they relied on you in planning their ceremony. Backing out because a higher-paying offer came along would be a breach of your obligation and would wrong them (and would also be deceptive if you gave a false excuse). You should not accept the gala at the expense of the wedding.
- If, for some unforeseeable and unavoidable reason beyond your control you genuinely cannot serve, you must tell them immediately, give a full refund, be transparent about the reason (not a lie), and make reasonable efforts to help them get replacement musicians. If you cancel for profit, you must not only refund the deposit but recognize that you have acted wrongly and should make appropriate restitution and seek reconciliation.
- About the “I’ll try to learn a second song” remark: that was a loose, non‑committal promise. That matters morally—don’t pretend you made a firm promise if you didn’t—but it still requires honesty. Tell the bride you were unable to prepare that extra song, apologize, and offer practical alternatives (play another piece you already know, hire/arrange another musician to do the song, use a recording for that one number, or learn it quickly if feasible).

Practical steps you can take (straightforward, honest, and charitable)
1. Decide now to honor the wedding booking. Call the gala and decline (or see whether they can hire you for another date or time). Your reputation and conscience are worth that.
2. Contact the couple as soon as possible (phone is better than email for pastoral tone). Say clearly that you are committed to their ceremony and will be there as agreed. That relieves them of anxiety and affirms your integrity.
   - Example: “We’re calling to confirm that we will be performing at your ceremony this Saturday as agreed. We’re looking forward to it and will be ready for your processional.”
3. About the second song, be honest and pastorally apologetic:
   - Example: “When I mentioned months ago that I’d ‘try’ to learn another song, I didn’t mean to give the impression that I had definitely learned it. I haven’t had the time to prepare it properly. I’m sorry. Here are options: (a) I can play X piece I already know for the reception, (b) I can arrange for a recording of the song, or (c) I can bring in another musician who can perform it—whichever you’d prefer.”
4. If you’ve already told others you might cancel or have been tempted to conceal the reason, confess that temptation to God and, if necessary, to the couple (repentance and transparent restitution go together).
5. If you do break the contract (only for true impossibility), give a full refund promptly, help find competent replacement musicians, and compensate for any provable extra expense you caused—this follows the spirit of restitution in the Standards.

Pastoral encouragement
- The Westminster Standards urge Christians to act with integrity toward neighbors and to glorify God in their business. Choosing the higher short-term payment over a formed obligation undermines trust, wounds your clients, and harms your witness. Honesty, promptness, and willing service here will honor both your profession and your faith.

Relevant principle (Westminster): worship must be conducted only as God has appointed it (Westminster Confession of Faith, ch. 21). Will‑worship, inventions of men, charms or superstitions, and addressing created things as objects of worship are forbidden.   - He promises a “guaranteed” answer to a formula and a touched cloth, which is superstitious and substitutes a man‑made rite for prayer and faith in God’s appointed means.

What aggravates each; the one thing that most defines each

Short answer up front
- Yes: an ordination vow is a solemn promise made before God and the congregation and therefore continues to bind you morally. It is not something to be abandoned by “ghosting.”  
- That said, staying in an office while habitually neglecting its duties is also sinful and harmful; if you cannot faithfully discharge the office you should either seek restoration (counsel, a leave, renewed service) or resign openly and orderly.  
- The informal promise to “help look at the books” is not the same as being a treasurer, but it is still a promise you made; you ought either to fulfil it or to formally release the congregation from it by arranging a hand‑over or by confessing your inability and helping a transition.

How I reach that from the Westminster standards (in brief)
- The Westminster Confession and Catechisms treat church offices as instituted by Christ for the care and government of his flock and treat vows and promises seriously. Ordination is not merely a private arrangement but a public covenant and call to spiritual work (the Bible‑centred ordering of the church and care of souls is central in the Standards).  
- The Standards also insist on godly honesty and the keeping of promises, and on orderly church government (so that things are done with transparency and conscience before God). From those principles: vows should not be lightly broken; church order must be respected; and sin (including sloth, deceit, bitterness, or abandoning the flock) should be confessed and remedied.

Practical, concrete counsel (what you should do now)
1. Stop planning to ghost. Don’t. It would be deceptive and would leave the flock and the Session to pick up the pieces without notice. That is inconsistent with a covenantal ordination vow.  
2. Take an immediate, honest step: ask for a pastoral meeting with the pastor and/or the Session clerk. Say plainly: you are burned out, you are struggling, you have been neglectful, and you need help discerning whether you can recover and resume your duties or must step down. Ask for prayer and counsel. This models repentance and responsibility.  
3. Explore a short, defined leave first. The Session can grant a temporary reduction of duties or a sabbatical/leave of absence so you can rest, receive pastoral care/counseling, and address bitterness toward the pastor. The Session is the proper body to authorize such arrangements.  
4. If restoration is not possible, resign openly and orderly. A biblical, Westminster‑shaped resignation should include: a meeting with the Session (not a private “I’m gone” note), a brief statement of reasons without slander (e.g., “personal burnout and inability to perform the duties faithfully”), an apology for any neglect, and an offer of help with an orderly transition (dates, handing over files, turning over responsibilities). Let the Session make the public announcement and handle any necessary election/appointment.  
5. Regarding the bookkeeping promise: be transparent. If you actually agreed to help and can still do it responsibly, either complete the agreed work or set a short, concrete deadline for handing it over. If you cannot, tell the Deacons/Session you are unable and provide or help arrange documentation (access to files, notes, passwords, lists of transactions) and a recommended person to take it on. Don’t simply abandon the books—financial confusion is a concrete harm and ought to be avoided.  
6. Confess the selfishness/bitterness and seek restoration. The Standards call for repentance and restoration where sin has occurred. Confess privately to the Session and, if needed, publicly to those harmed. Accept whatever pastoral steps the Session judges fitting (counsel, suspension from office for a season, or orderly removal).  
7. If your frustration involves actual wrongdoing by the pastor, follow the church’s biblical and ordered processes (Matthew 18 pattern, appeal to Session/Presbytery as polity requires). Don’t let personal bitterness or private neglect substitute for the right procedures.

Suggested practical timeline and wording
- Immediate (this week): request a meeting with the pastor/Session clerk; state your need for counsel and either a leave or to discuss stepping down.  
- Short term (2–8 weeks): either take a leave for rest and counseling or, if you are resigned to leaving, prepare a short written resignation addressed to the Session: state your office, say you acknowledge having been negligent, that conscience and duty compel you to step down because you cannot faithfully perform the duties, ask their forgiveness, offer to assist a brief transition (give X weeks or offer to finish the bookkeeping work or hand over records), and ask the Session to make the appropriate public announcement. Keep personal criticisms of the pastor out of the public resignation—use Session processes for that.  
- If handling the bookkeeping yourself is impossible: provide the books and electronic access, a list of pending items, point someone to the bank files, and offer a one‑time meeting to walk through them; if you really cannot do even that because of burnout, say so—but then accept whatever the Session directs about turning things over.

A few pastoral cautions
- Don’t minimize the seriousness of vows, but don’t remain stubbornly where you are only out of pride. The Standards require conscience before God, repentance for failure, and orderly action.  
- Don’t air grievances against the pastor publicly; follow church order. If there are legitimate charges, bring them to Session or higher judicatories as your polity allows.  
- Get pastoral care and outside help for burnout (spiritual direction, counseling, rest). Many elders have been restored after seasons of exhaustion.

If you want, I can
- Draft a short, humble resignation letter you could use or adapt;  
- Draft a short request for leave to the Session; or  
- Suggest how to present a bookkeeping handover checklist so the congregation is not left at risk.

Summary
Your ordination vows still bind you; you should not ghost. But you are not required to remain in office while habitually failing to care for the flock—still, the right route is repentance, pastoral counsel, and an orderly, honest resignation or temporary leave. The bookkeeping promise is morally significant: fulfil it if you can, or formally release/relinquish it with a clear hand‑over so the church is not harmed.

Short answer up front: morally (and very likely legally) you are bound to the written order at $4,200. You must either complete the table and chairs for that price, or (if the buyers validly rescind) promptly refund their deposit and not hold it hostage. You do not have the right to unilaterally add a surcharge simply because your costs rose. You do, however, owe them timely, truthful communication about the delay and diligent effort to finish in a reasonable time; if they cancel after you have begun work they may justly be asked to cover your actual costs, but you should not demand more than is fair or keep their money without accounting for it.

Why (briefly, from the Westminster Standards): the Standards require fidelity to lawful promises and fair dealing with our neighbour; promises and bargains once freely made are morally binding, and wrongs must be made right by restitution. Using the deposit as leverage to impose a new price or secretly sell the work without fair accounting would conflict with those principles.

Practical steps to take now
1) Re-read the written order and any language about the deposit, cancellation, or time for performance. Note exactly what you promised in writing (price $4,200; deposit $2,100; no price-adjustment clause; no firm delivery date).  
2) Communicate immediately and frankly to the couple (phone + follow up in writing). Say what you told them verbally about the finish, explain honestly that your material cost unexpectedly rose, and give clear options (below). Do not demand more money without their explicit consent.  
3) Offer them fair, concrete options:
   - Option A: You complete and deliver the set at the agreed $4,200, absorb the cost overrun (you accept the business loss). If you choose this, give a realistic delivery date and a small courtesy (free delivery/assembly, minor upgrade, or a small discount on future work) to help preserve the relationship.  
   - Option B: Ask if they will agree to a revised price, but only if they freely consent in writing. If you present a revised price, show a clear, honest explanation of increased costs and offer to share the additional cost rather than passing all of it on. Do not pressure them.  
   - Option C: If they cannot or will not pay more, offer to cancel the order and refund the deposit promptly. If you have already incurred non-recoverable costs (lumber cut, parts made), be transparent about those costs and propose to deduct actual, documented costs from the deposit only if they accept that arrangement; better yet, refund the deposit and seek to recover your costs by selling elsewhere—ethically you should account and justify any deduction.  
   - Option D: Offer alternatives to keep the price: substitute a less expensive wood, simplify the design, or deliver later if a change of finish or cure period will reduce other costs.

4) On the Thanksgiving comment: because you said “I’ll try” rather than a firm promise, you did not contract to that date. Still, you owe prompt updates and reasonable diligence to finish. Apologize for the delay, explain the curing problem, and give a new realistic ETA.

5) If they cancel and you keep the deposit to cover work done, do a full accounting and offer their choice to either accept the accounting and let you keep the remainder, or to have a full refund if the deposit exceeds your costs. Do not keep the deposit as a punitive measure or to force acceptance of a higher price.

6) If you and the couple reach an agreement to change price or scope, document it in writing and get their signature.

What you should not do
- Do not send a unilateral “revised invoice” that claims a surcharge and treat it as mandatory. That is a breach of the bargain and would violate honest-dealing principles.  
- Do not threaten to sell the set to someone else while holding their deposit unless they have validly cancelled and you have accounted for costs. Selling the piece while keeping their money without consent would be unjust.  
- Do not conceal your costs or misrepresent facts to extract more money.

If this becomes a legal dispute
- Legally, whether you can keep the deposit, recover costs, or claim lost profits depends on contract law and the exact terms you signed; some jurisdictions treat deposits as liquidated damages or part payment, others permit recovery of reliance costs. Morally, the Standards require honest accounting and restitution where appropriate. If needed, consult an attorney, but pursue truthfulness first and litigation only as a last resort.

How to say this (sample script)
- “I want to be straightforward with you. Our written order is for $4,200 and I gave you that price. My material costs have risen unexpectedly and that leaves me absorbing about $1,400 more than I anticipated. I cannot unilaterally change the contract. I see three reasonable options: I can finish and deliver for the $4,200 as promised; we can agree on a revised price together (only if you freely agree in writing); or you can cancel and I will refund your deposit promptly (or, if you prefer, I can provide an accounting of the costs incurred and adjust the refund accordingly). I’m sorry about the delay with the finish; I will give you a new, realistic delivery date and keep you updated.”

Longer-term lessons (practical and consistent with the Standards)
- Add explicit price-adjustment language in future written orders (how material surcharges will be handled), a clear cancellation clause, and a firm deposit policy (what it covers and under what conditions it is refundable).  
- Build a cushion into bids for volatile-material jobs or require smaller lead times for priced-but-unordered materials.  
- Continue to practice transparent, faithful dealing; that preserves reputation and aligns with the moral teaching of fidelity to promises.

Summary
- You owe performance at the contracted $4,200 unless the customers freely agree otherwise. You must be honest about the delay and diligent to finish. If they cancel, refund the deposit unless you have a documented, fair claim for actual costs; in every case treat them fairly and account transparently. The Westminster Standards require you to keep promises and to make restitution for wrongs — the straightforward, honest approach above is what those standards would require.

Short answer: yes — you are morally bound to keep the price you promised unless you are genuinely excused by something that makes performance impossible; you must not invoke a clause you know does not apply or take advantage of the cafe’s need for your gain. At the same time the Standards do not demand that you ruin yourself to keep a bargain; if performance has become truly impossible you may be excused, but you must act honestly, seek a fair solution, and make restitution for any wrongful gain.

Why, from the Westminster Standards (summary):
- The moral law requires truth, faithfulness in vows and bargains, and justice toward our neighbour. The Confession and Catechisms repeatedly treat covenants, promises and oaths as serious duties before God; Christians are to keep their word and not defraud others.  
- The same documents require care for one’s own household and stewardship of possessions, so one is not commanded to destroy oneself to keep a promise.  
- Where sin has been committed (breaking a promise, falsehood, exploiting another) the Standards require repentance and restitution.

Practical counsel
1. Read the contract carefully and get legal/contract advice about the force‑majeure wording. Many force‑majeure provisions excuse non‑performance only for things that make performance impossible (war, natural disaster, government act), not mere economic hardship or price increases. If the clause genuinely applies, follow its terms (notice, mitigation, etc.). If it does not apply, you are not free to invoke it dishonestly.

2. If the clause does not excuse you, treat the contract as binding. Morally you should keep the locked price for the remaining two months unless you have a legitimate excuse. Breaking it to sell to the higher bidder would be a breach and would be morally wrong under the Standards’ teaching about faithfulness and not defrauding a neighbour.

3. Negotiate openly and charitably. Before taking any harsh step, talk with the cafe owner and explain the situation honestly. Propose fair alternatives such as:
   - a temporary, modest price increase phased in over weeks;
   - reducing their weekly quantity at the $11.50 rate while offering additional supply at the market rate;
   - a short suspension with notice while you both look for alternatives;
   - helping them find a cheaper supplier or ways to reduce waste/usage.
Honest negotiation honors both your stewardship concerns and your neighbour’s dependence.

4. If, after good faith negotiation, you truly cannot perform without imminent ruin, then exit only in a frank, documented way and provide reasonable assistance/compensation for the damage you cause (help them find interim supply, give extra notice, pay reasonable switching costs). The Standards require making restitution or providing for the loss caused by your breach when you have taken advantage or caused injury.

5. If you do break the contract improperly and profit from it, you must make restitution and repent. The confessional teaching expects that wrongful gain be returned or compensated and that one confess and amend one’s ways.

How to proceed now
- Don’t secretly invoke force majeure or cancel to sell to the big cafe. That would be deceitful and unjust.  
- Consult your contract and a lawyer to know your legal position.  
- Then approach the cafe owner, explain the reality (cost increases and pressure), and propose concrete, equitable options (gradual increase, reduced quantities, temporary subsidy arrangement, or assisted replacement). Offer any reasonable help if you must terminate and consider compensating them for switching costs.  
- If you cannot avoid significant loss, pursue the least injurious option and be prepared to make restitution if a breach was wrongful.

Final pastoral note
The Standards urge that Christians be faithful in covenants because God is faithful; keeping promises and dealing justly is a form of worship. At the same time they recognize duties of stewardship and household provision. Pray, seek wise counsel, act transparently, and choose the course that honors God by being truthful, just, and compassionate.

Short answer first: you should not quietly treat your written commitment as flexible and simply take the tour dates. The Westminster Standards require fidelity to promises and duty to the church; so your first steps are immediate transparency with the committee and choir, seeking a formal release if one is to be given, and—unless you are released—doing everything reasonable to honor the commitment or to make good if you cannot.

How I reach that conclusion from the Westminster Standards
- The Standards repeatedly treat vows, oaths and promises as morally serious. Promises made to others are not to be broken lightly; Christians are called to fidelity and to perform “good works” in obedience to Christ and love of neighbor. (See the Confession’s teaching that oaths and vows are to be taken with seriousness, and the general teaching that Christians should perform duties in charity and fidelity.)  
- The Standards also affirm the Christian’s calling to use gifts and opportunities for God’s glory and neighbor’s good. So an important opportunity is not to be despised—but an opportunity to benefit you does not automatically supersede a prior obligation to your church without consent and just cause.

Put simply: keep your solemn, written, public commitment unless you obtain an church’s clear release or there is a weighty, justifiable reason that the church recognizes for you not to keep it. Quietly assuming it is flexible is a breach of trust.

Practical steps to take now
1. Tell the committee chair and music committee immediately (don’t wait). Be candid: explain the invitation, the dates that conflict, how meaningful the offer is to you, and that you did not intend to put anyone in this spot. Ask for their clear decision about whether they formally release you from the commitment for those dates (and, if needed, for the rest of the season).
2. Tell the choir promptly and pastorally. The singers deserve honest notice so they can adjust. Don’t spring this on them at the last minute; that would be unkind.
3. Offer concrete, immediate help to make the Christmas music happen without you if the committee chooses that route:
   - Train an assistant or designate a competent singer/conductor and give them all scores, markings, a rehearsal plan, and a recorded guide track you make for them.
   - Schedule extra sectional rehearsals you can lead before you leave, or run a full dress run earlier.
   - Provide detailed cues, tempi, and wording for the accompanist and instrumentalists; leave annotated parts and a click/tempo guide.
   - If necessary, help fund or hire a paid interim conductor or rehearsal/accompanist to lead the dress rehearsal and to run through the piece while you’re away.
4. If the committee refuses to release you, you must honor the original commitment unless there is clear, mutual agreement to alter it. If you break it anyway, confess and make restitution: apology, help to prepare replacements, and an offer to make good on costs or lost ministry fruit.
5. If you are released, get that release in writing (email is fine), and understand whether it applies only to specific dates or to the whole season. Clarify expectations about your broader season commitment (are you stepping down for the season, or are you simply absent for two dates?).
6. Reflect with your pastor and a trusted elder or mentor about priorities, reputation, and vocation. The Standards encourage submitting to church government and wise counsel.

How to decide if the tour should ever legitimately outweigh the prior commitment
- The tour could be the right choice only if the church (through its committee and leadership) releases you freely after understanding the impact, or if there is some weightier obligation or impossibility (e.g., sudden family emergency, a legal requirement, or something that makes you absolutely unable to fulfill the commitment). Your unilateral change of mind for professional advancement, by contrast, is ethically weak under the Standards.
- Consider also the fruit: will taking the tour serve the church’s good in some greater way (connections, testimony, resources) that the church recognizes? If so, the church might willingly agree to a release.

Sample language you can use right now
- To the committee: “I’ve been offered a guest-conducting engagement with a touring choir that conflicts with our dress rehearsal and Christmas Eve. I did not seek to create this conflict and I regret the timing. I will do everything possible to ensure the Christmas music goes forward well if you prefer that, but I will respect the committee’s decision. I ask you to let me know as soon as possible whether you will release me for those dates or whether you expect me to fulfill my prior commitment. If released, I will provide detailed materials and rehearsal help to ensure the program succeeds.”
- To the choir (if asked to inform them): “I have an unexpected professional opportunity that conflicts with our rehearsal schedule. The committee and I are working on a plan. I’m sorry for any worry; I’ll be back to explain the decision and to help as needed.”

Finally, posture and repentance
- If you find you were tempted to treat your prior promise as disposable for personal gain, confess that failing of heart to God and to those wronged; the Standards call Christians to humility and repentance when they have placed self-interest above duty.
- If you are released and go, conduct yourself in a way that honors your home church (speak positively, give thanks, help where you can when back). If you stay, embrace the ministry and lead sacrificially.

Summary
- Don’t quietly break a written, public commitment. Inform the committee and choir immediately. Seek a formal release if you are to be excused; if released, document it and provide full help so the service succeeds. If not released, honor the commitment and decline the conflicting dates. If you do break it without consent, confess and make restitution.

Short answer from the Standards: because you signed a fixed‑price quote that lists “packaging,” you must honor that covenant honestly. The Westminster standards teach that God’s moral law binds Christians to truth and justice in their dealings with their neighbour: we must keep our promises and not defraud or deceive. A covenant or contract entered into knowingly is to be performed or made right; you may not keep the money and withhold agreed deliverables because performance is harder than you expected. At the same time, the Standards allow and commend fair, charitable dealing: explain honestly, seek mutual agreement about any change in scope, and make restitution if you cannot perform.

What you actually owe now
- Deliver what the signed quote promises: the brand package including packaging (print‑ready dielines) unless performance is genuinely impossible. The clients trusted your written quote; that creates a binding obligation.  
- The “maybe throw in” social templates that were not written and were spoken as tentative are not a binding part of the written contract. If they now expect those because of your comment, you should be honest and clarify whether you will provide them (and on what terms), but you are not morally required to provide extra unrecovered work you never committed to in the signed quote.

What you should not do
- Do not withhold deliverables or misrepresent what you are delivering to keep the money. That would be to defraud them, which the Confession and Catechisms treat as sinful.  
- Do not take advantage of their limited English or vulnerability.

Practical steps to take now (honest, orderly, and charitable)
1. Review the written quote and list exactly what is stated as deliverables (logo, menu, signage, packaging — and what “packaging” means in that document).  
2. Communicate promptly, simply, and kindly. Because of the language barrier, use a translator, translated written summary, or a trusted bilingual person so there is no misunderstanding. Say something like:  
   - “I under‑estimated the time needed to create print‑ready packaging files. I want to honor our agreement. Here are options I propose so you get what you paid for and I can complete it without producing poor work or losing everything.”  
3. Offer clear options (pick one or present as choices):  
   A. Complete the full contracted set (including print‑ready dielines) for the original price, delivered on an agreed realistic schedule. (You absorb the loss this time.)  
   B. Deliver a simplified, printer‑ready version of the packaging that meets their immediate needs within the original price and offer to do more complex dielines for an additional fee (present a clear, reasonable extra charge).  
   C. If you really cannot complete the contracted work in any acceptable way, offer a partial refund proportionate to what you cannot deliver and deliver what you can; explain this honestly and apologize.  
4. If you choose to ask for more money for the additional work, present it as a request to amend the contract, not as a demand or a threat to withhold deliverables. If they decline, you should still perform the original written obligation or refund appropriately.  
5. If a timely solution requires subcontracting some technical dielines, offer to arrange that and pass any reasonable additional cost transparently to them, or pay the subcontractor and explain the cost to them.  
6. Document whatever you agree in writing and get their confirmation (again, with translator help).

How to handle your loss and conscience
- The moral thing is to honor your word or make restitution. If you must absorb some loss this time, do so and learn from it; that is consistent with the Standards’ stress on faithfulness and neighbourly justice.  
- You may legitimately protect yourself going forward: include clear scope, hourly rates for out‑of‑scope work, change‑order procedures, revisions limits, and a termination clause; require deposits and staged payments; and get agreements in a language the client understands.

A note on the friend’s advice
- The friend’s counsel to keep the money and withhold key deliverables is contrary to the duty to keep promises and to honesty. The Westminster Standards treat such deception and defrauding as sin. Do not follow that.

Practical wording you can use now (short)
- “I made a mistake in estimating the packaging work. I want to be fair and finish what we agreed. Can we talk (with translator) about these options: finish as agreed on a new schedule, do a simpler printer‑ready version and quote the rest separately, or if you prefer I can refund part of your payment? Which do you prefer?”

Finally, learn the lesson the Standards also teach: keep your covenants and act with honesty and charity; protect yourself in future contracts so you can be faithful without ruin. If you want, I can help you draft a short message to the owners (simple English + suggested translation) or sketch the exact options and a modest extra‑fee schedule to present to them.

Friday Night House Charter
(for the regulars of the weekly game & cigar night)

We are friends who come together for fellowship, laughs, and a good smoke. This charter is our mutual pledge — warm, straightforward, and meant to keep the night safe, fair, and respectful. By signing below you agree to the spirit and the letter of these points.

1) Buy-in and play responsibly
- The regular buy-in is $20. Keep it low. No one plays money he can’t afford to lose. We’re here for friends, not to bankroll someone’s bills or tempt someone’s finances.

2) Accommodation for Danny
- One of our own, Danny, has told us cards are a live snare for him as he continues his recovery. When Danny is present, there are no card games. We play dominoes, shoot the breeze, or just enjoy cigars and conversation. That compromise is non-negotiable — grumbling is allowed, undermining is not.

3) Conscience and liberty
- Poker is not treated by this group as inherently sinful, and we won’t turn the night into a place of legalism or judgment. At the same time, we affirm each man’s conscience and liberty before God. If a man chooses to stop or cut back because of his conscience, he will not be shamed or coerced. Out of charity and brotherly care we ask that such decisions be communicated openly (preferably privately first) so we can respect his space and not gossip. We expect honesty and accountability among brothers; if a member publicly abandons the group for reasons contrary to the covenant of fellowship without any private explanation, the group may request a respectful conversation to understand and preserve unity. Discipline, if needed, will be handled pastorally and privately.

4) Cars, debt, and safety
- We will help one another find good, legal deals on cars. No one is required to act as a broker or to put himself at personal or legal risk. Danny’s past and present situation must not be used as leverage or put him in harm’s way. If a member (including Danny) volunteers to help broker a legitimate, lawful cash sale, that is welcome — but only voluntarily, transparently, and with written agreement between buyer and seller. We will not participate in, encourage, or route business through illegal or coercive channels. Protect the man and obey the law.

5) Confidentiality
- What’s said at the table stays at the table. We do not repeat a man’s business around town. Confidential matters are handled discreetly and with care.

- Hosting and snack duty rotate. Each man takes his turn to host or to supply snacks, per the rotation list. If you can’t make your turn, arrange a swap with another brother in advance.

Kingdom Business Creed
(Framed over the lot — a pledge before God, my family, and my neighbors)

I, by God’s grace and under the Lordship of Christ, set this Creed upon my wall and bind myself to it as a rule of conscience and practice in the business entrusted to me.

1. Stewardship, Industry, and Profit
I acknowledge honest labor and lawful gain as gifts from God and tools for kingdom work. I will run this lot with ambition, thrift, and care, seeking profit not for selfish waste but to sustain my household, to bless others, and to advance Christ’s work. Hard work and honest profit are clean before God.

2. Honest Pricing, Shrewd Stewardship
I will price my vehicles with wisdom and market sense. A price is a price; I will not feign false bargains or manufacture scarcity. I will strive to be shrewd in stewardship — offering my best terms where bargaining is met and standing firm where buyers willingly accept the stated price — but I will do so without deceit, unjust advantage, or manipulation of the ignorant. Fair weights and honest measures shall guide every sale.

3. Truth in Dealing and Disclosure
All contracts, signs, and written statements I give shall speak the truth. Where I know of a defect, even if I sell “as‑is,” I will not conceal or silently profit from what I know will injure my neighbor. “As‑is” is not a cloak for fraud; it is an honest mode of sale when accompanied by clear disclosure of known faults. I will honor the implicit duty of neighbor-love that forbids taking advantage of another’s ignorance.

4. Warranties, Promises, and Reputations
I will keep my written warranties and all promises exactly as made. I will repair or make good where I have undertaken to do so. I will not slander, malign, or gratuitously disparage the dealer across town; I will honor the good name of others as I would my own.

5. Giving and Firstfruits
I will set apart the first tenth of each month’s net income to the local congregation and to the work of Christ before I draw a personal living. Generosity is a duty of grace and a testimony that my possession is stewardship, not lordship.

6. Prudence with Debt
I commit to pursue growth primarily by God‑given increase, thrift, and reinvestment. As a rule, I will avoid borrowing and will not take business loans lightly; I count a debt‑free operation a desirable testimony of trust in God. Recognizing Scripture’s call to prudence and justice, I will not dogmatize that borrowing is always a sin, but I resolve that loans will be a last resort, entered only after prayerful consideration, clear conscience, and a covenantal plan to meet obligations.

7. Conscience and Accountability
I will keep my conscience tender before God and submit to the oversight of Scripture and the fellowship of the saints. Where my practice fails to honor Christ, I will repent and amend. I will prize the glory of God above my profit and the good of my neighbor above short‑term gain.

By the grace of God, I sign this creed as the operating rule of my business and the solemn vow of my heart, that what I do at the lot be done as unto the Lord.

Short answer: By the Westminster Standards the elder who opposes binding uncommanded holy days is right as to what may be required of consciences in worship. You may teach about and commend historic seasons (Advent, Lent, Maundy Thursday, etc.) and you may use them pastorally as voluntary means of growth, but you must not make them required acts of worship or impose them on consciences the way the Lord’s Day and the sacraments are commanded.

Why (Standards and reasoning)
- The Confession teaches that the acceptable way of worshipping God is instituted by Himself in Scripture, and that men may not add to or take from what God has appointed. (See WCF, Ch. XXI; “the acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself… neither may men add thereto, nor take from it.”)  
- The Standards treat the Lord’s Day as the Christian Sabbath and the special divinely-appointed weekly day for public worship; they do not authorize the Church to create additional obligatory holy days. (See WCF, Ch. XXI; Shorter Catechism Q.98–Q.102 and the Larger Catechism on the Sabbath.)  
- The Second Commandment principle as set out in the Standards forbids human inventions in worship that would bind the conscience (i.e., enforcing rites, ceremonies or holidays not commanded in Scripture).

What the Standards allow (and how to apply that allowance)
- The Standards recognize that some “circumstances” of worship (time, place, order, musical expression, certain seasons used for teaching) may be adapted by church authorities for edification, provided they are not enforced as required worship and do not contradict God’s Word. Here the key is that such things remain adiaphora (indifferent) and pastoral expedients, not divine commands.  
- The Standards have historically permitted occasional public fasts and thanksgivings in response to providence; these are exceptional and circumstantial, not recurring holy days imposed as necessary means of grace.  
- Therefore it is lawful for the session to adopt a church teaching/calendar that uses Advent, Lent, Maundy Thursday, etc., as times for preaching, corporate instruction, or voluntary observance — but only as recommended, pastoral practices. Participation must be voluntary; no penalties or moral censure for non‑participation; nothing may be taught as required for salvation or as necessary worship.

Practical ruling you can present to the congregation (suggested wording)
- “Consistent with our subscription to the Westminster Standards, the Session affirms that the Lord’s Day and the sacraments are divinely appointed and required. The Session also recognizes the pastoral usefulness of the historic church seasons (e.g., Advent, Lent, Maundy Thursday) for instruction and spiritual growth. Accordingly, we approve adopting a church calendar for teaching and voluntary devotional practice, but we do not make observance of those seasons or days a requirement of worship or a matter that may be bound on the conscience. Any corporate observances (special services, imposition of ashes, memorial days) are to be offered as optional, with clear teaching that participation is not obligatory.”  

Pastoral cautions
- Avoid presenting saints’ days, ashes, or other rites as necessary marks of true holiness or as binding liturgical obligations; avoid rites that carry sacramental implications or imitate Romish usages in a way that confuses the people.  
- Make the voluntary nature explicit in all communications. Offer alternatives for those who conscientiously decline. Teach the biblical and confessional reasons for your approach so members understand both the pastoral value and the constitutional limits under the Standards.

If you want, I can draft a short formal motion for session/consistory to adopt (or reject) a recommended calendar with the precise confessional safeguards included.

Preamble
Whereas this congregation and its Session are bound by our subscription to the Westminster Standards and seek that all public worship be conducted “according to the appointment of Christ” and the rule of Scripture, these Standards are adopted to secure orderly, edifying, and theologically faithful worship. The Session, as the Lord’s undershepherds here, directs that every Lord’s Day service shall conform to these Standards. They are pastoral commands for the conduct of corporate worship in this church.

Definitions and Theological Principle
1. “Worship” shall be understood and ordered according to the Word of God and the principles of the Westminster Confession and Catechisms: God is to be worshipped only in ways appointed in Scripture; the ordinary means of God’s saving and sanctifying grace in public worship are the preaching of the Word, prayer, singing, and the sacraments (Baptism and the Lord’s Supper). Ceremonies and practices not commanded in Scripture must not be presented or used as conveying sacramental grace or as necessary for salvation or covenant standing.

Standards (binding)
1. Time, Length, and Order
  a. Public worship on the Lord’s Day shall begin at 10:30 a.m. punctually.
  b. Each regular Lord’s Day service shall be planned to conclude at 11:45 a.m. — a total service length of 75 minutes.
  c. The order of service for each Lord’s Day shall be prepared and approved in advance by the worship-planning team, reviewed by the pastor, and printed for distribution weekly. The printed order shall accurately reflect the service to be observed, and no unapproved deviation shall be introduced without the Session’s prior approval.

2. “Stations of Devotion” (8-minute segment)
  a. An eight-minute segment designated in the printed order as “Stations of Devotion” shall be scheduled in each service at the place indicated in the printed order (normally following the confession/assurance and prior to the sermon), and shall be faithfully observed in the printed form.
  b. The Stations shall consist of four simple, scripturally framed devotional tables bearing brief Scripture readings and short meditations composed and approved by the worship-planning team and reviewed by the pastor. The approved symbols for these tables shall be plainly described in the weekly printed order.
  c. The approved symbols may include a lit candle (symbolizing Christ as Light), a bowl of ordinary water used for a brief reminder of baptism (explicitly described as a symbolic remembrance), an object signifying anointing (kept for pastoral use only and not presented as a sacrament in public worship), and a table with a written meditation on prayer and confession. Language used at the tables shall make clear that these items are symbolic aids for prayer and meditation only.
  d. Participation in physically approaching or touching objects at any station is voluntary for worshipers. No act of touching, moving between tables, or any other gesture shall be represented, taught, or implied to “open the heart to receive grace” as if such touching were a means of sacramental grace apart from Word and ordained sacraments. Any teaching associated with the Stations must affirm that God’s grace is not conferred by objects or gestures but by the Spirit through the Word and the sacraments.
  e. The pastoral staff shall provide brief written guidance for all who may be uncertain about participation; minors shall participate only with parental consent.

3. Annual Covenant Renewal (Church Anniversary)
  a. On the church’s yearly anniversary an annual Covenant Renewal Service shall be observed, replacing the ordinary service for that Lord’s Day.
  b. The Covenant Renewal Service shall include: scriptural readings appropriate to covenant renewal, public prayer of thanksgiving and dedication, singing from the approved psalter-and-hymn list, and an invitation for public renewal of commitment to Christ expressed in spoken congregational covenant words prepared and approved by the Session.
  c. No physical rite of anointing or the public touching of oil as a rite shall be prescribed as an element of this service. Oil may be present in informational display for historical/theological instruction only, and, if used pastorally, only in private pastoral ministrations (e.g., James 5 pastoral anointing), not as a congregational rite.
  d. No “decree” shall be recited or enacted in this service that purports to bind time, the coming year, or persons in a manner that implies a magical or extra-biblical efficacy. The congregation may adopt a corporate prayer of dedication committing the church and its members to the Lord’s care and mission for the coming year; such language shall be framed as a prayer and vow, biblically grounded and voluntary in spirit, not as a binding incantation.

4. Sermon Placement and Length
  a. The sermon shall ordinarily occupy the final third of the service and shall precede the closing elements of worship (psalm/hymn of response, prayers, benediction).
  b. The sermon shall not exceed twenty-five (25) minutes in duration unless the Session grants a specific exception in advance for a particular service or teaching series.

5. Music and Singing
  a. Congregational singing shall be selected from the Session-approved psalter-and-hymn list. Solo, choral, or instrumental offerings must likewise be drawn from approved repertoire or receive Session approval in advance.
  b. Music selections shall be theologically faithful, declare Christ, edify the congregation, and avoid liturgical or devotional expressions that contravene the church’s confessional standards.

Enforcement, Review, and Exceptions
1. The Session is the final authority for the interpretation and enforcement of these Standards. The pastor and worship-planning team are charged to implement them faithfully.
2. Ministers, worship leaders, and volunteers shall receive orientation and written copies of these Standards. Services must conform; persistent and intentional deviation shall be addressed by the Session as a matter of church discipline in accordance with our polity.
3. Any proposed deviation or new liturgical element not expressly permitted herein shall be submitted to the Session in writing with theological justification and scriptural warrant. The Session may approve time-limited trials, but no element contrary to the principles set forth in the Preamble and Definitions shall be adopted.
4. The Session shall review these Standards annually and may amend them as necessary to guard faithfulness to Scripture and our confessional commitments.

Pastoral-Theological Note (for guidance to the worship-planning team)
These Standards are adopted in conscience under the rule of the Word, mindful of the Westminster Confession’s teaching that worship must be instituted by Christ and limited by His revealed will. While the Church may use biblical symbols and helpful devotions, it must never present objects or gestures as conferring grace apart from the ordinary means—the preached Word and the sacraments—nor introduce rites that resemble Romish ceremonies or imply superstitious efficacy. The purpose of all permitted devotional elements is to point sinners and saints alike to Christ, to lead the congregation into Scripture-shaped prayer, and to nurture holy reverence, not to invent new means of grace.

Article I — Definitions and Purpose

1.4 Purpose: To govern our conduct as partners in a manner that honors God, protects the company’s resources, and advances gospel work.

Article II — General Rule of Life and Business
2.1 All partners covenant to act with truthfulness, diligence, love, and fairness in all company affairs.
2.2 We will submit disputes, if not resolved among us, first to Christian mediation (see Article IX), and if necessary to the discipline and counsel of mature elders agreed to by the partners, that our witness may remain blameless.

Article III — Reserve Cash and Investments (Term 1)
3.1 Prohibition on interest-bearing custody: No partner shall deposit, place, or keep any portion of the Company’s Reserve Cash in an interest-bearing bank account, bond, investment fund, mutual fund, money-market vehicle, or any instrument intended to earn a financial return. Reserve Cash shall be held in plain cash or in non-interest-bearing custody only.
3.2 Security and custody: Reserve Cash shall be safeguarded: kept in a secured company safe or non-interest-bearing lockbox; withdrawals in excess of $_____ require the joint signatures of two partners; a written log of withdrawals and deposits must be kept and made available to all partners.
3.3 Exceptions: Petty cash for immediate small disbursements (under $___) and short-term escrow required by a contract (where interest-bearing custody is legally required and unavoidable) are permitted only with prior written approval of a majority of partners and must be fully disclosed to all partners.

Article IV — Opportunistic Acquisition of Competitor Clients/Crews (Term 2)
4.1 Duty to present opportunities: If a partner becomes aware of an opportunity to acquire a competing landscaping outfit’s client list, crews, assets, or contracts at a materially discounted price due to their hardship (including purchases from a former partner), that partner shall promptly present the opportunity in writing to all partners and shall not, without the company’s consent, privately acquire or divert the opportunity to himself or to a third party using company identity or resources.
4.2 Right of first pursuit: Upon written presentation, partners shall have [7] business days to evaluate and make a decision. During this period the presenting partner shall act in good faith to preserve the opportunity for the Company.
4.3 Procedure and decision: If a majority of partners vote in favor within the response period, the Company shall have the right to pursue the acquisition, and funds and management shall be allocated as agreed. If a majority declines or does not respond within the period, the presenting partner may proceed personally only after providing written notice to the partners and only so long as he does not use Company funds, reputational capital, or confidential information belonging to the Company to effect the acquisition.
4.4 Ethical restraint: Whether the acquisition is made by the Company or by an individual partner after the Company declines, all acts must be conducted with Christian integrity (no deceit, no inducement by false statements, and no breach of existing contractual duties).

Article V — Books, Records, and Honest Dealings (Term 3)
5.1 Honest books: Each partner will keep honest, accurate, and up-to-date Company books and records. No partner shall falsify, conceal, or misrepresent financial information.
5.2 Open inspection: All books, records, contracts, and invoices shall be open for inspection by any partner on reasonable notice. Monthly financial statements will be prepared and distributed to all partners.
5.3 Performance of contracts: The Company shall render to every subcontractor, supplier, and counterparty exactly what our written contract with them provides. No partner shall unilaterally alter contractual terms or withhold agreed payments without the express written consent of the partners.

Article VI — Compensation of Partners (Term 4)
6.1 Salary cap: No partner may take a salary greater than the regular wage paid to the lowest-paid field crew member of the Company at that time.
6.2 Test of heart: A partner who desires to draw a higher salary must (a) submit the request in writing; (b) before additional salary is paid, spend a full consecutive calendar month living on the lowest-paid field crew wage, demonstrating by testimony and observable life that his heart is free from the love of money and that he seeks to honor the Company and God; and (c) obtain approval by an affirmative vote of [at least three] partners (or unanimous, if the partners so require).
6.3 Reimbursement and special compensation: Reasonable expense reimbursements and one-time distributions tied to specific services or capital contributions must be documented and approved by majority vote and shall not be used to evade the salary cap.

Article VII — Giving to Gospel Work (Term 5)
7.1 Priority giving: Before any partner draws distributions of profit, the Company will allocate and distribute [10%] of Net Profit (hereinafter defined) to gospel work and Christian ministry designated by unanimous partner agreement. Net Profit for this purpose shall be determined according to the Company’s usual accounting practices, after operating expenses and the Reserve Cash target are met but before partner distributions.
7.2 Designation and oversight: Partners will agree each fiscal year on the specific ministries, charities, or church work to receive these funds. Disbursements will be transparent and recorded in the Company books.

Article VIII — Conduct Toward Competitors and Former Partners (Term 6)
8.1 No badmouthing: No partner shall badmouth, slander, or make false or misleading statements about any competitor or former partner in order to win business. Honest comparison is permitted; deceitful or malicious disparagement is forbidden.
8.2 Non-solicitation of current company contracts: A partner leaving the Company shall not solicit the Company’s clients or crews for personal gain in breach of this covenant during the period of separation as agreed in a separation addendum.

Article IX — Discipline, Remedies, and Restitution
9.1 Call to repentance: If a partner is alleged to have violated this covenant, the partners shall first seek private repentance and correction (Matthew 18:15–17). If unresolved, the matter shall be submitted to agreed Christian mediators or elders for counsel and reconciliation.
9.2 Restitution: If misconduct caused loss to the Company or third parties, the offending partner shall confess, make full restitution to the extent possible, and submit to such corrective measures as the partners, in counsel with Christian mediators or elders, deem Biblical and just.
9.3 Removal and buyout: Persistent, unrepentant violation of material covenant terms may result in removal by a unanimous vote of the other partners (or a supermajority as the partners may later adopt). In such case, the removed partner’s interest shall be bought out at fair book value as of the most recent accounting date, less any proven damages attributable to the partner’s breach. The buyout procedure shall be detailed in an agreed separation addendum.

Article X — Confidentiality and Use of Company Resources
10.1 Confidential information: Company financials, bidding strategies, pricing structures, client lists, and crew agreements are confidential and may not be used for personal advantage outside the Company without express written consent.
10.2 Use of company resources: No partner shall use Company funds, equipment, labor, or goodwill for personal acquisitions or ventures without prior written approval.

Article XI — Admission, Amendment, and Duration
11.1 Admission of new partners: New partners may be admitted only with the unanimous written consent of existing partners and upon signing this Covenant.
11.2 Amendment: Amendments to this Covenant that affect the moral terms (Articles III–VIII) require unanimous written consent of all partners after consultation with a panel of elders or Christian advisors agreed upon by the partners. Amendments to administrative matters may be made by a [three‑quarter] majority.
11.3 Duration: This Covenant continues so long as the Company operates or until dissolved by unanimous consent.

Article XII — Final Provisions and Signatures
12.1 Intent: We intend this Covenant to be a solemn promise before God and before one another to govern our business conduct. Partners acknowledge that this instrument is a religious and moral covenant; partners may also execute such legal documents as counsel advises to reflect commercial and statutory requirements, but recognize that the moral pledges herein are binding upon their consciences as Christians.
12.2 Severability: If any provision hereof is held invalid, the remainder shall remain in force to the extent consistent with our purpose of faithful stewardship.
12.3 Witness and signatures: In witness whereof we, the undersigned partners, bind ourselves herein before God and each other.
