We, the Session of [Congregation], being bound by our solemn subscription to the Westminster Standards and the Holy Scriptures, do hereby adopt as binding Worship Standards for all public services of this church. These standards are enacted to preserve the purity, reverence, and order of worship, to protect the consciences of the saints, and to promote orderly devotion according to the Regulative Principle of Worship. No practice in these Standards shall be understood to add to, alter, or teach contrary to the doctrine of Scripture as confessed in the Westminster Confession of Faith and Catechisms.

Enactment
Therefore, by the authority of the Session, the following Reverent Worship Standards are established as mandatory. All officers, leaders, members, and regular attenders are required to conform to them in every public worship service.

1. Weekly Covenant-Remembrance (explicit limitation)
- The church acknowledges the care of the saints for one another and encourages visible means of mutual encouragement. Members who have been given a small engraved wooden token at the time of their admission to membership may, at their own discretion, bring that token forward before the benediction and lay it in the designated bowl on the communion table while a leader offers a brief prayer of thanksgiving or intercession.
- Such an act is permitted only as a voluntary, external sign of personal remembrance, public profession, and mutual encouragement. It is expressly forbidden to teach, assert, or imply that the physical laying down of such a token effects, renews, or secures a member’s standing before God, or that omission from this practice renders any person “unsealed,” outside the covenant, deprived of the benefits of Christ, or otherwise disfranchised from the covenant community. Assurance of standing before God is by the work of Christ received by faith alone (as confessed in the Westminster Standards), and this congregation will not bind any outward act as necessary to obtain or retain covenant standing.
- Leaders who preside at such remembrances must instruct plainly that the sign is devotional and not sacramental in the sense of conferring grace apart from God’s appointed means; no language of “sealing” or “unsealing” shall be used in any doctrinal or disciplinary sense.

2. Bodily Decorum in Congregational Singing
- To preserve reverence and order in public praise, no member or attendee shall, during the corporate singing of the church service, raise hands, wave, sway, clench fists, or otherwise engage in visible bodily demonstrations of emotion within the sanctuary.
- Corporate singing is to be engaged with sobriety of spirit and with the inward devotion of the heart, expressed through voice and quiet demeanor, that others may worship without distraction. Exceptions of necessity (medical or physical need) shall be accommodated with pastoral discretion.
- Officers and worship leaders shall teach and model devotional engagement of mind and heart in singing consistent with the Confession’s emphasis on inward devotion and Scripture’s command to sing.

3. Time, Length, and Order of Service
- Public worship shall begin promptly at 10:00 a.m. and shall conclude within seventy (70) minutes except by express prior authorization of the Session or its delegated officers.
- Each service shall follow the fixed printed order approved by the Session. Variations to the printed order may be made only with the prior approval of the Session or its designated worship committee and shall be announced as such at the service’s outset.
- The printed order shall include stated times for Scripture reading, preaching, sacraments, prayer, singing, corporate confession, and benediction consistent with the Book of Church Order and the Westminster Standards.

4. Sanctuary Conduct and Children’s Attendance
- No beverages (including coffee) shall be brought into or consumed within the sanctuary during public worship. This rule is enacted to maintain cleanliness, order, and the solemnity of the worship space.
- Children under the age of six shall normally be cared for in the nursery during the main service. Parents who wish their children to remain in the service must obtain prior permission from the Session or its designated elders, who shall give such permission with pastoral sensitivity and according to the nursery and safety policies of the church.
- Nursery supervision, materials, and instruction shall reflect the church’s confessional commitments and catechetical concerns.

5. Approved Psalter and Hymnody
- All sung praise in public worship shall be drawn from the Session-approved psalter-and-hymn list. The Session’s approved list shall be consistent with Scripture and the doctrines of the Westminster Standards and shall be reviewed periodically by the Session.
- No other hymnody or musical texts shall be introduced into the public service without prior approval of the Session. Arrangements, musical settings, and instrumentation shall be submitted to and approved by the Session’s worship committee for conformity with the church’s doctrine and the orderly conduct of worship.

Implementation, Teaching, and Enforcement
- The Session appoints the Worship Committee to implement these Standards, to prepare the printed order, to maintain the approved psalter-and-hymn list, and to train worship leaders, musicians, and officers in their faithful observance.
- Enforcement shall be pastoral, not punitive: officers shall seek to instruct, correct, and restore with patience and charity; willful and persistent violation after admonition shall be referred to the Session for appropriate pastoral correction according to the Scriptures and the church’s discipline.
- Nothing in these Standards shall be interpreted to bind the conscience in a matter of doctrine contrary to the Westminster Standards: where a question arises as to doctrine or practice touching the means of grace or the chief ends of worship, the Confession and Catechisms shall govern.

Adoption
These Reverent Worship Standards are presented for the Session’s vote and, upon adoption, will be posted and distributed to the congregation. They shall take effect on the Lord’s Day following their adoption unless the Session directs otherwise.

Signed for and by the Session of [Congregation], on this day [date].

Fair & Charitable Reference Policy (Binding)
Purpose
We are committed both to treating departing colleagues with kindness and to preserving the trust and reputation of our firm and of our client and partner community. This policy sets a simple, binding standard for the content and format of references given by managers on company letterhead. It is written in a spirit of charity and integrity: charity toward departing employees, and honesty toward any firm or person receiving a reference.

Scope
This policy applies to all managers and supervisors who may be asked to provide written references, recommendations, or employment verifications for current or former employees of [Firm Name].

Policy (binding)
1. Do not cite weaknesses. A manager’s written reference must never include mention of a departing employee’s weakness, failure, or “growth area.” References are not the place to catalogue shortcomings; charity requires that we not needlessly injure a person’s future opportunities.

2. Affirmation, limited by truth. Managers are expected to write warmly affirming references when they can do so truthfully. When the facts permit, managers should affirm departing employees using positive phrasing (for example: “strong,” “a great hire,” “highly recommended”). However, managers must not put words into a reference that they know to be false. If a manager cannot honestly make such affirmations, they must not sign a letter stating the falsehoods; instead they must follow the neutral/reference-handling procedure in Section 3 or notify HR for guidance. (See Section 5 below for consequences of knowingly false statements.)

3. Protecting partners and avoiding deception. If a manager genuinely believes a prospective hire would pose a material risk to a partner firm, the manager must not attempt to convey that concern by knowingly deceptive means. The manager has two appropriate options:
   a. Provide a neutral, factual employment verification (dates, title, basic responsibilities) only; or
   b. Decline to provide a detailed character reference and refer the requester to HR for an official statement.
If the manager believes a partner firm should be warned because of documented misconduct or risk, the manager must raise that concern confidentially with HR (and provide any supporting documentation) so the firm can respond appropriately. Under no circumstance should a manager intentionally write something that they know to be false or intentionally mislead by calculated deception; omissions that are used as a device to produce a materially misleading impression are inconsistent with this policy.

4. Form and signature. All references on behalf of the firm must be:
   - On official [Firm Name] letterhead;
   - Dated; and
   - Signed by the manager of record (the manager who supervised the employee or who is designated by the firm).
If a manager is unable to sign a truthful, affirmative reference, they should forward the reference request to HR and sign only if they can comply with this policy’s requirements.

5. Truth requirement and accountability. No reference may assert, in writing, anything the manager knows to be false. Managers must certify, by signing the reference and by signing this policy acknowledgement, that to the best of their knowledge the statements in a reference are accurate and not knowingly false. Knowingly making false statements in a reference is prohibited and will result in disciplinary action, up to and including termination.

Procedures
- All incoming written reference requests should be forwarded to HR upon receipt. Managers may draft a reference consistent with this policy and share it with HR before sending.
- When in doubt about wording, managers must consult HR. HR will provide standard neutral verification language for managers to use when a truthful, affirmative reference is not possible.
- If a manager believes a departing employee poses a risk that should be disclosed to a prospective employer, the manager must notify HR with any relevant documentation; HR will determine the firm’s official response and legal exposure.

Enforcement
This policy is binding. Managers who violate Sections 1–5, particularly by knowingly making false statements in a reference, will be subject to corrective action or disciplinary measures up to termination. Managers are required to sign the Acknowledgement below before providing any reference on firm letterhead.

Rationale (brief)
This policy is designed to honor two duties that we hold as a firm: the duty of charity toward departing colleagues (avoid gratuitous harm) and the duty of truth toward those who rely on our statements. Charity must not be an occasion for falsehood. Where strict truthfulness and charity appear to conflict as to particular phrasing, managers must err on the side of not inventing praise and must use the neutral/HR-handled options provided.

Short answer up front, according to the Westminster Standards:

- Ben: yes — his practice, as described, conforms to what the Fourth Commandment requires. Outwardly he rests from his ordinary calling, devotes the day to worship and thankful delight, foregoes business preparations that would force work on the Lord’s Day, and his helping the stranded motorist is exactly the sort of “work of necessity and mercy” the Standards allow. Inwardly his delight and reverence for the day show the required heart-attitude.

- Cara: no — her keeping fails the commandment. The Standards require an outward keeping of the Lord’s Day (ceasing from ordinary worldly employments and engaging in public and private worship); working through the morning worship hours without necessity is a breach of that outward duty. Her sincere inward sense of “rest” while working does not excuse contravening the command.

What the Westminster Standards actually say (brief paraphrase and application)
- The Fourth Commandment is a continuing moral duty and is to be kept holy by Christian people in the Lord’s Day (the first day of the week). Keeping it includes resting from ordinary worldly employments and recreations, attendance on public and private worship, the reading of Scripture and private and family prayer, thanksgiving and spiritual rest of soul, and allowing others the like liberty. (WCF ch. 21; Larger and Shorter Catechisms on the Fourth Commandment.)
- The Standards expressly allow “works of necessity and mercy” on the Lord’s Day (helping the needy, relieving immediate danger, necessary sustentation, etc.). They do not allow ordinary business, convenience, or preference in place of the day’s duties.

Applying those points to each person

Ben
- Outward observance: He closes his store, attends worship, prepares in advance so business duties do not bleed into Sunday, and takes a peaceful family meal. That is precisely the kind of outward discipline required. His stopping to help a stranded motorist is squarely a lawful work of necessity/mercy and so is not forbidden.
- Inward disposition: He delights in the Lord’s Day as a gift and does not reduce it to legalistic nitpicking about minor pastimes for his children. That delight and charity toward neighbor are the inward obedience the Catechisms expect. One pastoral caveat: “not policing” must not become laxity that allows ordinary worldly employments or patterns that routinely displace worship or holy rest; but on the facts you gave, Ben is doing what the Standards require.

Cara
- Outward observance: By staffing and personally working the morning worship hours without necessity — when she could reasonably have covered those hours — she is not resting from her ordinary worldly employment and is failing to observe the public worship duties the Standards require. The provision for “necessity and mercy” does not cover doing business for convenience or preference during the appointed time of worship.
- Inward disposition: The Standards require both outward and inward obedience. Sincere inward “attitude” or inward rest does not relieve the obligation to keep the day holy outwardly. So, even if Cara sincerely believes she is “resting inwardly,” that inward feeling does not make a disobedient practice acceptable. The Catechisms condemn substituting an inward sentiment for God’s explicit outward command.

Practical pastoral counsel
- To Ben: Continue in what you are doing. Keep preparing in advance so the day is not compromised, cultivate family and personal worship and teaching, and continue to allow works of mercy where needed. Be watchful that “not policing every game” does not drift into treating ordinary employment and secular pursuits as indistinguishable from holy rest.
- To Cara: Encourage her to rearrange work so she is not working through worship hours except for genuine necessity or mercy. If the business must serve those who truly have no other access (real necessity), operations should be limited to what that necessity requires and not be an occasion to evade public and private worship. Pastoral instruction should stress that the Lord’s Day requires both the outward cessation from ordinary callings and the inward delight in God; both matter.

Final note on sincerity and obedience
The Westminster Standards are clear: the moral command stands and requires both outward observance and inward conformity. Sincerity of feeling or intention cannot turn a contrary outward practice into obedience.

Household Covenant for the Lord’s Day

Preamble
We bind ourselves as a household to keep the Lord’s Day holy, setting it apart each week for rest, worship, and family devotion. This covenant is given in love and obedience to the Lord, and in reliance upon the Biblical and Reformed teaching we receive in the Westminster Standards: that the Lord’s Day is to be sanctified for worship and holy rest, and that works of necessity and mercy are not to be profaned (Westminster Confession, and the Larger and Shorter Catechisms). We enter this covenant deliberately and willfulness, as a family under God, to keep our home from common profanation of the day.

Accordingly we covenant as follows. These are binding rules for everyone living under this roof.

1. No routine helping or errands outside the home on the Lord’s Day
- Principle: Sunday is to be a day of cessation from ordinary labor and of devotion to God. Therefore, except for genuine emergencies, family members will not undertake errands, drive other people, or otherwise engage in outward acts of assistance that pull us into ordinary weekday activity.
- Exception (per Scripture and the Westminster Standards): Works of necessity and acts of true mercy for urgent need are permitted. If a life, health, or safety emergency arises (for example: serious medical emergency, immediate danger to life or property), anyone may and must respond as needed, and must notify Dad as soon as practicable. For non-urgent requests from neighbors or relatives, we will decline or defer to a weekday; children are not to be sent to assist others on the Lord’s Day.
- Practical application: If you are unsure whether something is an emergency, stop and call Dad. If Dad is unavailable, use your best judgment with mercy and prudence.

2. Quiet, careful supervision of the children; play restricted to restful, orderly activities
- Principle: The Lord’s Day is not a day for ordinary exertion or for profane recreations. Children will be watched and guided to keep their activities calm, reverent, and restorative.
- Rules: Running, rough-and-tumble play, strenuous sports, or hobby projects that look or feel like work are to be set aside on the Lord’s Day. Quiet games, reading, family devotions, gentle board games or walks of worshipful reflection (if led by an adult) are acceptable.
- Enforcement: Parents will supervise the children’s activities all day. If an activity escalates into what is properly “work” or excessive exertion, it will be stopped and replaced by a quieter alternative.

3. No household shopping, laundry, or paid work on the Lord’s Day; family worship prioritized
- Principle: Ordinary household chores and paid employment are to be set aside on the Lord’s Day so we may keep the day holy and enjoy family worship and rest.
- Rules: Shopping, running household errands, doing laundry, and conducting paid business are not to be done on Sunday. We will set aside time together for family worship, Scripture reading, prayer, and attending corporate worship as a family.
- Practical provisions: Plan weekly chores, shopping, and work schedules so they are completed on weekdays. If unusual, unavoidable business matters arise, notify Dad immediately for direction.

4. Father’s discretionary “Flex Sabbath” with limits
- Principle: While we hold Sunday as our set day for worship and rest, Dad may, under his discretion, declare a particular Sunday a “flex Sabbath,” shifting our primary rest day to another day that week. This is exercised for substantial, planned reasons (for example: an unavoidable business peak that cannot be otherwise met).
- Limits and responsibilities:
  - Flex Sundays will be the exception, not the rule, and will be announced in advance.
  - Even when a flex Sunday is declared, the spiritual obligations of the Lord’s Day remain: we will still attend our church’s corporate worship that Sunday (or, if circumstances make that impossible, we will make special provision for family worship at another appointed time), and we will not treat the change as a license for lawless or profane activity.

Short answer
- Elmwood: Clean. Their screen and clock are lawful circumstances (prudential aids), not additions to the instituted elements of worship.
- Crossroads: Not clean. A mandatory “Covenant Renewal Ceremony” that is invented, taught as a means of grace, and enforced as a condition of membership is an unlawful addition to worship.

Reasoning from the Westminster Standards (summary)
- The basic norm in the Standards is the Regulative Principle of worship: the acceptable way of worship is that which God has appointed in His Word; we must not add to or take from what Scripture has instituted in worship. The Confession and Catechisms recognize the instituted elements (reading and preaching of the Word, prayer, sacraments, singing/praise, and giving) as worship elements commanded or warranted by Scripture. At the same time the Standards allow for "circumstances" (times, place, order, helps and expedients) to be ordered by prudence so long as they do not introduce new rites or change the prescribed elements.
- Two errors to avoid: (1) Equating any modern convenience with an illicit addition to worship. Prudential aids that do not alter the content or nature of the instituted elements are generally lawful. (2) Accepting a church’s mere assertion that an added practice is “warranted” as sufficient. If a practice is not an instituted element and functions as a religious rite (taught as means of grace, required, or enforced by ecclesiastical penalty), it is an unlawful addition.

Application to each case

(A) Elmwood
- Matter (what is done): Elmwood keeps the instituted elements—Scripture read and preached, prayer, sacraments, congregational singing, giving. Nothing added to the content.
- Manner (how it’s done): The elders use a projected sermon text and hymn words and display a fixed starting time on a screen/clock. Those are aids to hearing, corporate participation, and punctuality. They do not pretend to be sacraments, nor are they presented as spiritual means of grace, nor do they change culpability or standing in the covenant.
- Verdict: Clean. According to the Standards, projecting text and showing a clock are circumstances ordered by prudence. They are lawful provided they remain aids and do not become required rites or replace instituted elements. If someone’s conscience is troubled, the proper remedy is pastoral conversation and explanation (and, if necessary, seeking conciliation by the session/presbytery), but the use itself does not violate the Regulative Principle.

(B) Crossroads
- Matter: Although Crossroads retains the usual instituted elements, the elders have added a monthly, mandatory “Covenant Renewal Ceremony” invented by them, in which members re-sign a loyalty pledge and are taught that the rite is a means of grace and necessary for membership standing.
- Manner: The ceremony is presented as a spiritual rite, required for membership and taught to confer spiritual benefit; dissent is treated as rebellion against God-ordained authority. That makes the practice an imposed religious rite with coercive consequences.
- Why this is unlawful under the Standards:
  - It is a human-invented rite, not one of the instituted sacraments or other Scriptural acts of worship; making such a rite part of corporate worship violates the Regulative Principle.
  - Teaching it as a “means of grace” and requiring it for membership attaches spiritual benefit and ecclesiastical penalties to a human invention, which the Standards condemn.
  - Treating dissent as rebellion against God-ordained authority improperly elevates human ecclesiastical practice above Scripture; the Standards require that all church practices be judged and bound by Scripture, not by asserted authority.
- Verdict: Not clean. The addition is an unlawful innovation in worship and an abuse of ecclesiastical authority.

Practical counsel (what to do)
- For Elmwood’s situation: Encourage the member to speak privately and humbly with the elders/session about their concerns; the elders can explain the prudential rationale. If the disagreement persists and is conscience-bound, seek mediation under the church’s normal courts. But removing such lawful circumstances is not required by the Regulative Principle.
- For Crossroads’ situation: Members who object should raise the matter with the elders/session and demand a scriptural warrant for making the ceremony a required worship rite and membership condition. If the session persists, the matter should be brought to the presbytery or higher church court under the standards’ judicial processes. The Standards require restoration to scriptural worship; if officers continue to introduce and enforce unwarranted rites, that is a grievous error requiring correction, and members may be relieved from participating until the practice is rescinded. If ecclesiastical remedies fail, prudence may require wider appeal or separation for the sake of faithful worship.

Bottom line: the Standards allow prudential circumstances (Elmwood’s screen/clock) but forbid invented, coercive rites treated as means of grace or required for membership (Crossroads’ ceremony).

6. Tokens and symbolic placement (each places a token on the table then takes it again as a reminder) (5–8 min)
7. Prayer of blessing and pastoral commitment (5 min)
8. Optional: Lord’s Supper (if your fellowship practices it and leadership deems appropriate) or time of prayer/laying-on-of-hands (10–15 min)
9. Closing benediction and practical next steps (5 min)

Setting and atmosphere
- Room dimmed, single soft spot on the “altar” table; simple, reverent instrumental music playing low as people enter.
- On the table: a plain bowl or small plate, a chair for leaders, an open Bible, a lit candle (optional, as a sign of Christ’s presence but not as an object of devotion).
- Tokens: a simple item you can hand each person as a physical reminder: a small smooth pebble, a wooden cross token, or a printed card with a Scripture and pledge on it. Emphasize its role as a mnemonic—not a sacrament or charm.

Leader roles
- Lead Pastor / Principal Leader: delivers exhortation and leads the covenant vow, prays blessing.
- Two Assistants: hand out tokens, guide people, help with practicals and pastoral follow‑up.
- Music leader: plays simple, reverent instrumentals and leads any singing.
- Pastoral follow up team: meets new members one‑on‑one afterward to discuss commitments and plan discipleship.

Script (word‑for‑word text you may use)

[Before people sit] (music fades; room quiet)
Leader (standing near the table):
“Good evening. Tonight is a time to give thanks for what God has done in bringing you here and to solemnly place yourselves before Him in a covenant of mutual commitment. We dim the lights and quiet our hearts not to create mystery for its own sake, but to set our minds on one thing: the presence and promises of God.

We will read Scripture, hear a brief exhortation, and then make a personal vow before the Lord and each other. You will receive a small token as a tangible reminder of this vow. Let me say plainly: the token is only a reminder. It does not save you. Your hope is in Christ alone and in the ordinary means of grace—God’s Word, prayer, the fellowship of the saints, and the sacraments rightly administered. We invite you to speak the vow aloud to the Lord three times. The repetition is for emphasis and solemnity, not magic.

Let us begin by listening to God’s Word.”

Scripture reading (Leader or reader):
“Read Romans 8:28–39 and Philippians 1:3–6.” (You may print and distribute the texts.)
(After reading)
Leader:
“These passages remind us that God who began a good work in you is faithful to complete it. Our covenant tonight is not to manufacture that faith, but to place ourselves under God’s covenantal care and the means He gives—so that by grace we may persevere.”

Short Exhortation (Leader; 8–12 minutes)
Leader:
“Friends, God calls sinners to Himself and graciously gives perseverance to those He effectually calls. Our hymnody and the Scriptures rightly fill us with awe. Yet Christian life is not a private sentiment; it is covenantal. We join to Christ, and we join with one another in a mutual life of prayer, instruction, worship, and discipline. That is the framework of the life we promise to live.

Tonight you will vow to live within that covenant—relying on God, receiving the means of grace, being accountable in love, and submitting to pastoral care. That vow is not a new sacrament. It is a solemn promise before God and the church. We do this because God calls us to deliberate commitment and because the church is a means God uses to nurture and keep his people.”

Silent reflection (2–3 minutes)
Leader:
“Take a moment to quiet your hearts. Think of the promises you are about to make and the grace you seek from the Lord.”

The Covenant Vow (printed copies available; leaders give brief instructions)
Leader:
“I will lead you now in the vow. When it is your turn, speak it aloud to the Lord and the congregation. We will repeat it three times in total: I will say it once, then you repeat it once, then we all say it together once. If you are uncomfortable saying your name aloud, you may simply say ‘I do’ or speak your vow quietly to the Lord. This is a vow, not a pledge to a person. Say it as you intend it before God.”

Vow text (use exactly or adapt):
“I, [Name], relying on the grace of God in Jesus Christ, solemnly covenant before God and these brothers and sisters: to seek Christ by prayer and the Word, to participate faithfully in the life of this fellowship, to submit to loving shepherding and mutual accountability, and to strive for holiness by God’s grace. I ask for God’s help and the prayers of this church. Amen.”

Procedure (lead):
- Leader speaks the vow aloud once line by line; participants repeat.
- Repeat the vow a second time with participants speaking it themselves.
- Third time: leader invites everyone to say it together.

Tokens and symbol (handing out tokens)
Assistant (quietly passes tokens as the vows finish):
“As we hand you this [stone/wooden token/card], know what it is and what it is not. It is a reminder of the vow you have made and of God’s promises. It is not a sacrament, it is not an amulet, and it does not carry a mystical power. Keep it to help you remember this night and to return your heart to Christ when you need reminding.”

Symbolic placement (optional physical action)
Leader:
“We now place our tokens briefly on the table as a sign that we commit these promises to the Lord and to one another. You may place your token in the bowl and then take it back as a reminder, or, if you prefer, leave it in the bowl for the first week as a visible sign of this covenant.”

(Participants come forward in an orderly way, place token in bowl, receive it back or leave it—direction depends on your preference. Play soft instrumental music.)

Prayer of blessing and assurance (Leader)
Leader (hands extended):
“Heavenly Father, we thank You for calling these brothers and sisters to Yourself. Grant them, by Your Spirit, faith to hold fast to Christ, steadfastness in the face of trial, and zeal for holiness. We do not promise their preservation; You do. We ask that You, who began a good work in them, would complete it. Guard them, keep them, and make this church a place of grace where they are instructed, corrected, and loved. We commit ourselves to them in shepherding and discipleship. Through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.”

Pastoral commitment and practical steps (Leader)
Leader:
“As leaders, we pledge to walk with you. Within the next week a pastoral leader will meet with each of you to discuss your covenant, your spiritual growth, and a plan for regular discipleship (a Bible study, mentor, accountability partner, and the meetings you are to attend). If you ever lose or discard the token, do not treat that as a spiritual failure—it is only a reminder. If you struggle in your faith, come and tell us so we can pray and bear your burden.”

Optional: Lord’s Supper / Imposition of hands / Personal prayer
- If your fellowship practices the Lord’s Supper and this is an occasion appropriate for it, celebrate it in a biblically faithful manner. Otherwise, offer laying on of hands and prayer for those who desire it. Make clear: these are pastoral practices and means of grace; they do not confer automatic sanctity.

Closing benediction (Leader)
Leader:
“May the God of peace sanctify you wholly; and may your whole spirit, soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. The Lord who began a good work in you is faithful to finish it. Go in peace and in the fellowship’s love; we will walk with you. Amen.”

Practical leader’s guide and cautions

1) The token is a reminder, not a sacrament
- Rehearse leaders to say explicitly, several times, that the token is a mnemonic device only. If at any point you hint the token “secures” faith or “seals” calling by virtue of human ritual, you cross into superstition.

2) On repetition
- Repeating the vow three times is permitted as emphasis and solemnity, but do not make the number three a magical requirement.

3) On assurances and language
- Do not say phrases such as “the anointing has now sealed your calling and God will not let you drift” as though the leaders’ anointing or a ritual guarantees perseverance. Instead, teach the doctrine of God’s preserving grace (e.g., “The God who began a good work will carry it on” — Philippians 1:6) and pray for that grace.

4) Resist manipulation
- Do not use language that suggests people “must” stay in the fellowship because of this ritual. Membership should flow from discipleship and love, and pastoral oversight should include “exhortation, affection, instruction, and discipline” (in line with Reformed pastoral practice), not coercive rites.

5) Follow‑up is essential
- Within one week, arrange one‑to‑one meetings to form discipleship connections.
- Provide a clear pathway for newcomers: small group assignment, meeting schedule, reading plan, and an accountability partner.

6) Pastoral sensitivity to conscience
- Some will be uncomfortable with public vows; allow private vows or quiet affirmation.
- Make sure no one feels coerced or shamed if they cannot attend or speak aloud.

7) Use of Scripture and catechetical teaching
- Pair this service with teaching on assurance, calling, covenant, and the means of grace. Use catechism or short teaching sessions to ground new members in doctrine (e.g., on God’s covenantal faithfulness and the ordinary means of grace).

8) If you celebrate the Lord’s Supper
- Only do so if your fellowship has the appropriate doctrinal and pastoral preparation. The Westminster Standards treat the sacraments as means of grace instituted by Christ. If you celebrate the Lord’s Supper, follow a careful, biblical liturgy and pastoral instruction beforehand.

Sample music and readings
- Music: low, reverent instrumentals (hymn tunes played on piano/violin/guitar), or a simple sung stanza of a classic hymn (e.g., “Before the Throne of God Above” or “O Church Arise” toned down). Keep it reverent.
- Readings: Romans 8:28–39; Philippians 1:3–6; Hebrews 10:19–25; Psalm 139:23–24; Galatians 2:20. Short catechetical summary about covenant and calling (one page).

Final notes for leaders (pastoral posture)
- Keep the emphasis on God’s promises and on mutual commitment to the life of the church.
- Be humble, sober, and pastoral. A solemn tone is good; theatricalism or quasi-magical language is not.
- Be prepared for pastoral moments (tears, confessions, doubts). Receive these graciously and arrange follow up.

- draft a leader’s checklist and schedule for the one‑week follow‑up meetings,
- or prepare a short catechetical talk (5–8 minutes) about assurance and the means of grace based on passages and Reformed doctrine.

Worship-Integrity Standard — [Conference Name]

Preamble
We convene to glorify God, to hear and obey His Word, and to guard the souls entrusted to us. In light of the duty of faithful worship taught by the Reformed confessions — that the acceptable worship of God is instituted by Him and confined to what He prescribes, and that ministers must not employ human inventions or deceptive practices in worship — this Standard sets binding rules for every conference session. These rules are pastoral, theological, and disciplinary: they protect congregations and uphold the integrity of Word-centered worship.

1. Public reading of Scripture
- Every session shall OPEN with the public reading of Scripture. A clearly audible, unabridged reading from the Bible shall precede announcements, teaching, or response times. The reading may be led by the presiding minister or a person authorized by the session leader and shall not be abbreviated or treated as a mere formality.

2. Prohibition of sensory-manipulation elements
- No instrumental music, no artful or atmospheric lighting, and no fragrances, incense, candles, scented diffusers, or any olfactory elements of any kind shall be used, displayed, or distributed in any session.
- No stage design, projection design, or visual effect intended to create an atmosphere or to evoke emotion by aesthetic means shall be employed. Lighting and visuals are permitted only to the extent necessary for clarity of sight and the reading of text (e.g., adequate house lighting, clear projection of Scripture text or logistical information) — not to create mood or ambience.
- No sound design, sub-bass, or musical amplification intended to produce a physiological or affective response shall be used. Audio may only be used to ensure clear speech audibility.
- Rationale: Worship must call hearts to the Word and to God Himself, not to manufactured sensory experience. Anything intentionally designed to stimulate the senses in order to induce or amplify emotion in a worship context is disallowed because it substitutes created means for the ordained means of grace and risks manipulation of conscience and affections.

3. Prohibition and remediation of engineered “Encounter” experiences
- Any session, room, or program that employs engineered lighting, sub-bass, scent, binaural/psychophysical sound, or other technological/architectural design expressly intended or A/B-tested to induce a physiological awe or trance-like response is strictly forbidden.
- Any facilitator or leader shall not employ a fixed script or any form of verbal suggestion that attributes attendees’ physiological or emotional responses to the “manifest presence” of God, or that represents such responses as God’s confirmation of a person’s calling, election, or decision.
- Explicit prohibitions:
  - No use of intentionally engineered sensory environments (lighting shows, low-frequency sub-bass pulses, scent stimuli, etc.) to create or amplify spiritual experience.
  - No scripted suggestive language attributing bodily or emotional reactions to divine confirmation, special revelation, or guaranteed spiritual states.
  - No experimentation (A/B tests, covert trials, psychological conditioning) on attendees without full, informed consent documented in advance.
- Remediation for existing programs:
  - Any Encounter Room or similar program in operation must cease the prohibited practices immediately upon the adoption of this Standard.
  - Program leaders must submit a written remediation plan within 14 days describing how the space and methodology will be altered to comply (remove sensory hardware or disable/lockout the offending elements, rewrite facilitator materials, cease any testing/data collection on unconsenting attendees).
  - All facilitators and staff of such programs shall undergo theological review and training supervised by the Worship Integrity Board before resuming any activity associated with the conference.
  - Any prior public claims that physiological responses constituted the direct manifest presence of God or constituted confirmation of calling must be retracted publicly and pastoral care offered to those who may have been harmed or misled.
- Rationale: Purporting technological or psychological inducement as a sign of God’s presence or as divine confirmation is deceptive and pastoral malpractice. Under the Westminster teaching against will‑worship and spurious revelations, ministers may not present induced sensations as divine proof.

4. Giving
- All financial giving at sessions is voluntary. No leader, speaker, or staff member shall exert pressure, use coercive language, stage manipulative appeals, or link giving to spiritual favor, blessing, or status. Clear, dignified means for voluntary giving (collection boxes, online links) may be provided with neutral explanation and no public pressure.

5. No engineered altar-call spectacles
- No session may stage an altar-call or decision-time that is designed or choreographed to manufacture responses (e.g., staged testimonies, suggestive cueing of crowd behavior, timed lighting/sound to prompt movement, confederates in the audience). Open invitations to respond in repentance or faith may be offered only when they arise organically from faithful preaching and are conducted with pastoral sobriety and privacy safeguards.
- Invitation language must be straightforward and rooted in Scripture; it must not be employed as a means to ramp up numbers or emotional impression.

Accountability, compliance, and enforcement
- Worship Integrity Board: A standing board (ministers and elders appointed by the conference leadership and accountable to the conference council) will receive reports, review compliance, and adjudicate violations.
- Attestation: Every session leader must sign a compliance attestation upon registration that the session will adhere to this Standard.
- Reporting: A simple confidential reporting channel will be provided for attendees, staff, and presenters to report suspected violations.
- Sanctions: For confirmed violations the Board may require:
  - Immediate cessation of the offending practice and public correction.
  - Mandatory theological/pastoral training for responsible leaders.
  - Suspension of the session’s participation in the conference, removal from future programs, or revocation of speaker privileges (depending on severity).
  - Where deception or pastoral abuse is found, notification of the speaker’s home church or denominational authorities for appropriate further discipline.
- Random and scheduled spot-checks may be conducted by the Board to ensure ongoing compliance.

Pastoral protections and care
- Where individuals report that they were misled or harmed by prior sensory- or emotion-manipulating practices, the conference will provide pastoral care, investigation, and appropriate public correction or apology as needed.
- The priority of this Standard is spiritual protection: honesty before God and neighbor, the rule of Scripture in worship, and the prevention of practices that could confuse the workings of conscience or the ordinary means of grace.

Short, plain commitments for session leaders (to post on program sheet)
- Opening Scripture reading will precede the session.
- No instruments, mood lighting, scented elements, or engineered soundscapes will be used.
- No experiential scripts will claim physiological feelings as God’s manifest confirmation.
- Giving is voluntary; invitations will not be staged manipulations.

Relevant standard and rule of judgment (from the Westminster teaching)
- The oath one takes invokes God as witness to the truth of what one says; it therefore requires truth and sincerity, not mere verbal accuracy. The moral duty under the commandment against false witness includes not only avoiding outright falsehood but also avoiding equivocation, secret reservations, deception by implication, and withholding material facts with the intent to mislead. Intention of the speaker and the obligation to make known what one knows that is material to the question are decisive. (This is the consistent emphasis of the Confession and Catechisms on oaths, the ninth commandment, and against equivocation and mental reservation.)

How I read the particular oath here
- The oath added the word “complete.” That makes explicit what the Standards imply: you must give what you know that is material to the matter, not merely utter isolated true sentences to produce a false impression.

(A) Fatima
- Matter axis (factual content): kept. Her answers are true; she volunteers a material fact the regulator did not know.
- Manner axis (intention, candor, non‑deceptive conduct): kept. She states honestly what she knows and what she does not know; she does not invent or speculate to fill a gap. Saying “I don’t recall” when she genuinely does not recall is an honest, non‑deceptive answer and consistent with the duty of truth under oath.
- Verdict: kept the oath. Her testimony fulfilled both the letter and the spirit of the oath as understood by the Westminster standards.

(B) Grant
- Matter axis (factual content): superficially kept (each sentence true), but materially broken. Although each isolated sentence is true, he knowingly withholds and arranges truthful statements to create a false overall impression about what actually happened.
- Manner axis (intention, candor, non‑deceptive conduct): broken. He deliberately answers the literal question rather than the question meant, uses true statements to mislead, lies by implication, practices mental reservation/equivocation, and delays or overwhelms with irrelevant true detail to prevent discovery of the truth. Under the Standards this is sinful deception and a violation of the oath: the heart’s intention to mislead renders the testimony dishonest.
- Verdict: broke the oath. He violated the “complete” duty of the oath and the ninth commandment’s prohibition of deceit and equivocation.

Practical counsel (pastoral/legal)

- To Grant: the proper course, according to the Standards, is to acknowledge the deception, correct the record to the regulator, and confess and repent for having used truthful but deceitful speech under oath. If there are legal consequences, cooperate with remedying the false impression you created.

Short summary
- Literal truth is necessary but not sufficient. The oath required truth and completeness of what one knows; Fatima kept both, Grant satisfied only literal truth while violating the spirit and duty of the oath by intentional deception.

Short answer up front

- Priya: No—on the facts you give she has not sinned against the tenth commandment in any continuing, condemning way. Her first, fleeting sting was a temptation/feeling which she did not willingly cherish but confessed and mortified; by morning her heart genuinely rejoiced. That is the pattern of repentance and grace the Standards require.

- Tom: Yes—he has. The Westminster standards make clear that the tenth commandment forbids inward motions of envy, grieving at the good of our neighbour, and rejoicing in his misfortune. Tom’s settled resentment, secret wish that Aisha stumble, and the private tally are exactly the inward sins the commandment condemns. The guilt lies primarily in the heart (though outward hypocrisy is also blameworthy and will bring further judgment if persisted in).

Why (from the Westminster teaching)

- The Decalogue is a law of the heart, not merely of outward behaviour. The Westminster documents insist the tenth forbids “all inordinate motions and affections to anything that is his” and requires “full contentment with our own condition” and rejoicing in another’s good. Sin is not only a public act but also consenting, cherishing, and delighting in evil desires.

- There is a further nuance the Standards recognize: involuntary tempting thoughts or momentary stirrings are not the same as consenting sin. What makes an inward motion sinful is the will’s consent, cherishing it, brooding on it, and allowing it to frame one’s affections and intentions.

Applying that to your two coworkers

- Priya: She felt a natural sting and admitted “I wanted it.” Because she did not entertain and cherish that desire, but honestly confessed it to God, resolved to mortify it, and by morning truly rejoiced and remained content, her inward disposition is consistent with the duties of the tenth commandment. On these facts the sin was not consummated; what occurred was a temptation followed by repentance and renewed obedience.

- Tom: Outwardly blameless behaviour does not absolve him. His private, settled resentment, enjoyment at the thought of Aisha stumbling, and keeping a secret tally show consenting inward affections of envy and malice. Those affections are precisely what the tenth forbids. The verdict of guilt sits in the heart; his outward courtesy only deepens the hypocrisy, but the core sin is internal.

Practical counsel to offer them (brief, biblical and consistent with Westminster pastoral practice)

- To Priya: Give thanks and keep watch. Continue the honest practice you have—confession, thanksgiving, and renewed service. Cultivate contentment by thanking God for his gifts, praying for Aisha’s success, and remembering providence. If the temptation returns, refuse to entertain it—biblical mortification of the flesh and renewed delight in God’s wisdom are the way forward.

- To Tom: Call him to repent. He should confess the sin to God (and to a trustworthy Christian friend or elder for accountability), forsake the inward habit (stop keeping the tally, stop rehearsing resentments), and pursue active love for Aisha—pray for her, seek to serve her honestly, and replace grudging comparison with gratitude and contentment. If he has acted on his tally or undermined her, he must make amends where possible. Left unchecked, inward envy will harden and ruin conscience and fellowship.

Final pastoral note

The Westminster Standards press that the heart matters supremely. Never be satisfied with merely polite outwardness; the law requires humble, thankful contentment and rejoicing in another’s good. At the same time remember the gospel-lens the Standards insist upon: where there is true repentance and dependence on Christ’s grace, God forgives and renews the heart.

Workplace Worship & Reverence Covenant

Preamble
We are a company founded on Christian conviction and committed to honouring Christ in our common life. In keeping with Scripture and our convictions, we seek a workplace shaped by reverence, mutual respect, and voluntary corporate worship. This Covenant sets expectations for participation in corporate worship and for the appearance of personal workspaces so that the whole company may be formed in gospel-shaped devotion without forcing consciences or doctrinal affirmations.

Agreement
As a condition of continued employment at [Company], I voluntarily enter into this Covenant and agree to abide by the standards and processes herein.

1. Morning Scripture & Prayer Gathering (voluntary)
- The Company will host a daily 15-minute Scripture-reading and prayer gathering each morning (the “Morning Gathering”). Participation is purely voluntary and open to all employees.
- The Morning Gathering will be resourced by the Company (Scripture readings prepared, prayer guides available, a clearly posted schedule and virtual option for remote employees).
- Employees may attend or skip the Morning Gathering without adverse effect on their employment status, evaluations, promotion eligibility, compensation, or standing with the Company, subject to the provisions of Clause 3 (timekeeping and aggregated engagement reporting).

2. Workplace Display Standard — “Reverent Desk” policy (mandatory)
- To cultivate a workplace oriented to Christ, personal workspaces (desks, cubicles, and immediate desk-area walls or partitions) shall not display items the Company reasonably classifies as “worldly celebration” items, including but not limited to birthday cakes kept at a desk, sports-team mugs or team flags, concert posters, or other non-religious memorabilia or celebratory paraphernalia that draw public attention to secular loyalties.
- Permitted desk displays are limited to: (a) an unobtrusive single Scripture verse or Scripture-based devotionals, (b) company-issued items, or (c) no display at all. Employees may choose between displaying a single Scripture verse or maintaining a neutral desk—their personal free choice.
- Enforcement: People Ops will conduct scheduled desk-appearance checks (with reasonable prior notice—standard initial notice 7 days). On first noncompliance, People Ops will notify the employee in writing and provide 7 calendar days to remove prohibited items. Failure to comply after notice will result in progressive corrective action up to and including termination, consistent with Company corrective-action policies.
- Religious Accommodation: An employee who believes a particular item is an expression of a sincerely held religious conviction (including items required by their own faith tradition) may submit an accommodation request to People Ops under the Company’s Religious Accommodation Procedure. People Ops will consider such requests promptly and in good faith and will grant reasonable accommodations unless they create undue hardship or conflict with the essential character of this Covenant.

3. Timekeeping for Morning Gathering and Engagement Reporting (logged; aggregated)
- To encourage visible corporate worship and to resource the Morning Gathering properly, attendance will be recorded in the Company timeclock/app when an employee attends a Morning Gathering.
- Recorded attendance will be used for administrative and resourcing purposes and will be included in the Company’s quarterly engagement reporting as an aggregate participation metric (company-wide and team-level participation rates). - Individual attendance records will not be used as a direct negative factor in individual performance evaluations, compensation decisions, promotions, or disciplinary actions. The Company reserves the right, however, to consider patterns of conduct that otherwise violate Company policy or work obligations (for example, habitual tardiness or failure to meet required job hours) under ordinary performance-management procedures.
- Transparency: Employees may view their own attendance logs in the timeclock app. If any employee has a conscientious objection to being logged, they may request an exemption; People Ops will grant a logging exemption where needed and will still record participation anonymously for aggregate engagement counts.

4. No doctrinal test as condition of employment
- The Company will not require employees to affirm any doctrinal statement, theological confession, or creed as a condition of hire, continued employment, promotion, or company membership. Participation in theological teaching, membership in Christian groups, or joining company-sponsored ministry teams is voluntary and not a condition of employment.

5. Desk decoration: Scripture verse or nothing
- Employees may decorate their desks with a single, unobtrusive Scripture verse (printed or framed) or may choose to have no desk decoration at all. This is a matter of personal choice and will not be used as a measure of religiosity or a condition of employment.
- Scripture verses must be consistent with Company standards of civility and not display inflammatory or divisive content. People Ops may decline display of a particular verse only if it violates workplace civility standards, and the employee will be offered an opportunity to select a different verse.

6. Compliance, Appeals, and Review
- People Ops administers and enforces this Covenant. Enforcement will follow Company corrective action processes with progressive steps and opportunity to cure noncompliance.
- Employees may appeal disciplinary actions relating to this Covenant by submitting a written appeal to People Ops within 7 calendar days of notice of discipline. Appeals will be heard by a committee that includes People Ops and a designated senior leader not involved in the initial decision.
- This Covenant will be reviewed annually by People Ops in consultation with the Founder and legal counsel to ensure faithful implementation, fairness, and legal compliance.

7. Respect for Conscience and Liberty of Worship
- The Company acknowledges that matters of worship and conscience are morally weighty and that Scripture and our confessional heritage require that worship not be coerced. Where a conflict exists between an employee’s conscience and the application of a particular clause here, People Ops will engage in prompt, charitable, and confidential discussion to seek a biblically faithful and legally compliant resolution.

Safety & Worker‑Dignity Policy
Purpose
Our workers’ safety, health, and human dignity are primary company obligations. This policy establishes binding standards to protect workers from heat and other hazards, to eliminate production practices that demean or coerce, and to ensure honest, prompt reporting and non‑retaliation.

1. Access to drinking water, shade, and paid rest breaks (binding)
- Reachable drinking water and shade: The company will provide potable drinking water and shaded resting areas within 50 feet of every workstation during all shifts where workers are exposed to heat or sun. These locations will be maintained, clearly marked, and replenished as needed.
- Paid rest breaks: The company guarantees paid rest breaks on a regular, published schedule that accounts for workload and environmental conditions. Break schedules are to be respected; employees may take additional safety/rest breaks when conditions or personal health require them (see Section 3).
- Reasonable accommodations: Supervisors must promptly arrange additional shade, cooling, or rest time where weather, task intensity, or a worker’s condition make it necessary.

2. Abolition of oppressive individual line‑speed quotas and punitive performance metrics; replacement with dignity‑centered standards (centerpiece—binding)
- Prohibition: The company abolishes fixed individual line‑speed quotas, punitive attendance‑linked bonuses, and one‑sided productivity metrics that create per‑employee pressure to work in unsafe conditions or to forgo rest. Such metrics are deemed inherently demeaning and incompatible with worker dignity and safety.
- Replacement approach: The company will use safety‑first, team‑based performance frameworks that:
  - Prioritize safe operation and well‑being over raw throughput.
  - Set production planning with input from workers and supervisors, ensuring targets are achievable without compromising safety or required breaks.
  - Use balanced metrics that measure safety compliance, quality, and team outcomes rather than punitive individual throughput only.
  - Avoid pay structures that penalize legitimate medical absence or rest breaks; any incentive programs will be voluntary, safety‑neutral, and designed with worker representatives.
- Review and worker participation: All production standards and incentive schemes must be reviewed and approved by a joint management‑worker safety committee. Changes to production practices that affect workload or rest must be communicated in advance and are subject to committee review.
- Enforcement: Violations of this clause (imposing oppressive quotas or punitive metrics) are a formal company policy breach and subject to corrective action, up to and including dismissal of managers who impose or maintain such practices.

3. Immediate response to injury/heat illness and prohibition on pressuring resignation or discouraging reports (centerpiece—binding replacement for requested clause)
- Immediate care and support: Any worker who is injured or experiences heat illness will receive prompt, appropriate medical attention and, if needed, transportation to medical care at the company’s expense.
- No coercion to resign; support for claims: Supervisors and HR are strictly prohibited from encouraging or pressuring any worker to resign, quit, or otherwise abandon a claim to avoid recording an incident. The company will assist workers in filing internal and regulatory reports and in accessing medical and legal resources as requested.
- Paid time and protections for reporting: Injured workers will be provided paid time for medical care and to complete any necessary reports or claims. Workers will not lose their position, seniority, or benefits for filing an incident report or claim that is made in good faith.
- Transparent encouragement to report: Supervisors will be trained to explicitly authorize rest and medical breaks, to encourage reporting of hazards or illness, and to document when breaks or aid are requested and provided. Supervisors must not use veiled language or implied threats about “numbers” to discourage workers from taking breaks or reporting injuries.
- Documentation and internal case handling: All injuries and heat‑related incidents will be documented in the company’s incident log within 24 hours and evaluated for corrective action. Workers will be informed of the documentation and of their rights to file regulatory claims.

4. Non‑retaliation (binding)
- Retaliation prohibition: Supervisors and employees at all levels are prohibited from retaliating against any worker for reporting a hazard, requesting a break for health/safety reasons, or filing an injury claim. Retaliation includes termination, demotion, pay reduction, adverse scheduling, harassment, coercion, or any adverse action.
- Remedies: Any worker who believes they have been retaliated against may file a complaint with HR and the company’s safety committee. Proven retaliation will result in disciplinary action (up to termination) for the retaliator and remediation for the harmed worker, including reinstatement and back pay where appropriate.
- Confidential reporting option: The company will provide a confidential reporting channel for safety complaints and suspected retaliation.

5. Honest and prompt reporting to regulators and internal transparency (binding)
- Prompt external reporting: The company will report workplace injuries, heat illnesses, and other reportable incidents honestly and promptly to the appropriate regulatory bodies in accordance with applicable law and within required timelines (and in any case within 24 hours of recognizing a reportable incident).
- Internal transparency: The company will maintain incident logs and make aggregated, de‑identified safety metrics available to employees and the joint safety committee to promote openness and joint problem solving.
- No concealment: Any attempt to conceal incidents, delay required reporting, or instruct workers not to file valid reports is a serious policy violation that will result in disciplinary action and possible legal consequences for responsible managers.

Implementation, training, and enforcement
- Safety Officer and committee: The company will designate a Safety Officer responsible for implementation and compliance and will maintain a joint management‑worker safety committee to review conditions, metrics, and proposed changes.
- Supervisor training: All supervisors will receive mandatory training on this policy, on recognizing and responding to heat illness and injury, on lawful reporting obligations, and on respectful communications that promote dignity.
- Audits: The company will conduct periodic audits to ensure compliance with this policy and applicable law. Non‑compliance will be remedied promptly and documented.

Worker protections
- Workers retain the right to seek outside medical care, to file regulatory claims, and to consult with legal counsel. The company will not impede these rights.

Effective date and enforcement
- This policy is company‑wide and binding from the effective date. Managers and supervisors are accountable to enforce it; violations by management will be treated as severe misconduct.

Family Stewardship & Succession Covenant
Preamble
We, [Sibling A], [Sibling B], [Sibling C], and [Sibling D] (the “Siblings”), heirs, stewards, and co-owners of [Company Name] (the “Company”), enter this Covenant in humble dependence on our Lord and in the spirit of mutual love, justice, and stewardship. We commit to care for our parents, sustain the business for future generations, and to avoid covetousness, deceit, and the family fractures that arise from unfair advantage.

Article I — Purpose
1.1 Purpose. To provide for the lifelong care of our parents, ensure responsible operational stewardship of the Company, protect equity rights of each Sibling, and create binding governance, transparency, and dispute-resolution mechanisms.

Article II — First Charge: Parents’ Care
2.1 Parents’ Care Fund. The Company shall establish and maintain — as the first corporate charge superior to distributions to owners — a Parents’ Care Fund sufficient to provide for our parents’ housing, medical care, long-term care, personal needs, and any reasonable ancillary expenses, for the remainder of their lives.
2.2 Funding and Priority. Annual budget and cash flow plans will allocate amounts necessary to meet the Fund before any dividends, owner draws, or owner distributions. In any year requiring extraordinary contribution to the Fund, Siblings shall treat such contributions as permitted capital calls per Article VIII.

Article III — Operating Sibling Compensation and Role (Heart: Anti-Covetousness)
3.1 Compensation Waiver. [Operating Sibling’s name] (the “Operating Sibling”) hereby waives any separate operating salary, owner-operator premium, management fee, or other preferential financial compensation for services rendered to the Company, except:
  a) Reimbursement of reasonable, documented out-of-pocket expenses incurred in the course of business approved under the Company’s expense policy; and
  b) Any change to this waiver requires unanimous written consent of all Siblings after full disclosure and reasonable deliberation, or a binding vote pursuant to Article IX (dispute resolution).
3.2 Share Equity. The Operating Sibling shall hold an equal economic ownership share as the other Siblings (e.g., one-quarter each), except as otherwise lawfully and freely transferred with competent consent as described in Article IV. The Operating Sibling agrees to discharge managerial duties as fiduciary and steward, subject to oversight from the Company board and the transparency provisions below.
3.3 Fiduciary Standard. The Operating Sibling shall at all times act as fiduciary for the Company and the other Siblings, keeping full and accurate records and acting for the common good rather than private advantage.

Article IV — Equity Transfers, Capacity, and Operational Continuity (Ethical and Binding)
4.1 Principle. Any transfer or restructuring of ownership that would materially change economic or voting control of the Company (including any transfer of 50% or more of equity to any single Sibling) shall be valid only if:
  a) Made freely by the transferring Owner while competent; and
  b) Documented in a written instrument executed in the presence of independent legal counsel for the transferring Owner and notarized; and
  c) Accompanied by a contemporaneous written certification of competency by a licensed medical professional chosen by mutual agreement (or, if mutual agreement is not reached, by a neutral medical examiner selected under Article XI); and
  d) The transferring Owner acknowledges, in writing, that they understand the nature and consequences of the transfer, after being given reasonable opportunity to seek independent advice.
4.2 No Exploitation. Any attempt to secure a material transfer when the transferring Owner’s capacity is substantially impaired, or any effort to secure a signature by manipulation, coercion, deception, or while the transferring Owner lacks sufficient understanding, is null and void as a violation of this Covenant and subject to injunctive relief and damages.
4.3 Operational Continuity Mechanisms. To ensure continuity while protecting rights:
  a) Management Agreement. The Siblings shall adopt a Management Agreement appointing the Operating Sibling as the Company’s manager (CEO/President) with clearly defined duties, authorities, and performance metrics. The agreement shall grant operational control sufficient to run the business day-to-day but not to unilaterally alter ownership without the procedures of 4.1.
  b) Voting & Board Structure. The Company shall adopt a board structure and voting rules that permit efficient decision-making (including provisions for a casting vote for the Operating Sibling on day-to-day operations if unanimously agreed now), while protecting owner economic rights and requiring the procedures of 4.1 for ownership changes.
  c) Temporary Emergency Authority. In the event of an acute emergency for which immediate action is necessary to preserve the Company, the Operating Sibling may take emergency measures reasonably necessary to preserve going-concern value; such measures must be reported in writing within 72 hours to the Siblings and ratified within 30 days by a majority of Siblings (excluding the Operating Sibling if conflict of interest exists) or by independent arbitration per Article IX.

Article V — Respecting Parents’ Wishes
5.1 Controlling Wishes. To the extent our parents, while competent, have clearly and contemporaneously expressed a distribution plan (by will, trust, or other properly executed instrument) that affects Company ownership, that document shall govern distribution and succession, provided the instrument meets the competency and execution standards of Article IV.
5.2 Preservation of Intent. If there is any ambiguity about a parent’s intent, Siblings shall in good faith seek to determine and effectuate the parent’s stated and probable wishes in consultation with independent counsel and, if needed, a neutral factfinder.

Article VI — Transparency, Books, and Audit
6.1 Open Books. The Company shall maintain accurate, GAAP-compliant books and shall provide quarterly financial statements to each Sibling within 30 days of quarter-end.
6.2 Independent Audit. An independent auditor selected by unanimous agreement of the Siblings or, failing that, by an independent arbitrator under Article IX, shall conduct an annual audit and shall make a written report available to all Siblings.
6.3 Valuations. Any valuation used for buy-sell, transfer, or distribution shall be conducted by an independent appraiser agreed by the Siblings or selected under dispute-resolution procedures.

Article VII — Non-Exclusion; Charity of Dissenting Vocations
7.1 No Automatic Forfeiture for Vocational Choices. No Sibling’s choice of lawful vocation (including ministry or other full-time public service) shall by itself forfeit or diminish that Sibling’s ownership rights. Any change in ownership by a Sibling who wishes to step away from the business shall be by voluntary, documented transfer under Article IV or by agreed buy-sell terms in Article VIII.
7.2 Good Faith Acknowledgement. The Siblings affirm that different callings and life choices are to be honored; disputes over contributions shall be resolved according to this Covenant’s procedures rather than by unilateral exclusion.

Article VIII — Buy-Sell and Capital Calls
8.1 Buy-Sell. The Siblings shall adopt a buy-sell agreement providing mechanisms for voluntary purchase or sale of shares, funding options, and right-of-first-refusal among Siblings, using independent valuation methods.
8.2 Capital Calls. Capital calls for Company needs, including extraordinary contributions for the Parents’ Care Fund, shall be made pro rata to ownership unless otherwise unanimously agreed.

Article IX — Dispute Resolution and Enforcement
9.1 Internal Resolution. The Siblings agree first to seek resolution by good-faith negotiation; if that fails, they will submit to mediation with a mutually agreed mediator.
9.2 Binding Arbitration. If mediation fails, disputes shall be resolved by final, binding arbitration under the rules of [arbitration body] in [jurisdiction], with arbitrator authority to order specific performance, injunctive relief, and monetary damages.
9.3 Interim Relief. Nothing in this Covenant prevents any Sibling from seeking interim injunctive relief from a court when necessary to prevent irreparable harm (including the prevention of exploitation of a vulnerable parent).

Article X — Legal Advisers and Independent Counsel
10.1 Independent Counsel for Parents. Prior to any ownership transfer that materially affects parents’ interests, the parents must be advised by independent counsel who certifies in writing that the parent has received independent advice.
10.2 Sibling Counsel. Each Sibling shall have the right to independent legal counsel at their own expense.

Article XI — Medical Competency Determination
11.1 Neutral Examiner. For any question of capacity under Article IV, the Siblings shall select a neutral medical examiner by unanimous agreement or, if unanimity is not possible, by the arbitrator named under Article IX.
11.2 Standard. Competency determinations shall be in accord with prevailing medical and legal standards in the jurisdiction.

Article XII — Miscellaneous
12.1 Binding Nature. This Covenant is binding on the Siblings and their heirs, assigns, and legal representatives, subject to lawful amendment by unanimous written agreement.
12.2 Governing Law. This Covenant shall be governed by the laws of [State/Jurisdiction].
12.3 Severability. If any provision is invalid, the remainder shall remain in force.
12.4 Execution. This Covenant becomes effective upon signatures of all Siblings and is intended to be enforceable by the Siblings in court or arbitration.
